**Surah al-Dhariyat (The Scattering Winds)**, sixty verses, Meccan

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By the winds that scatter with dispersal,﴾ ﴿and those that carry a heavy load,﴾ ﴿and those that run with ease,﴾ ﴿and those that distribute by command.﴾

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By the winds that scatter with dispersal,﴾ ﴿and those that carry a heavy load,﴾ ﴿and those that run with ease,﴾ ﴿and those that distribute by command.﴾

The beginning of this surah is connected to the end of what precedes it. When the Exalted explained the gathering (al-hashr) with its proofs and said, ﴿That is a gathering upon Us, easy,﴾ and said, ﴿And you are not over them a compeller,﴾ meaning, you do not compel them or force them into faith, this indicated their persistence in disbelief after the proof had been established and the Qur'an recited to them. Nothing remained but the oath, so He said: ﴿By the winds that scatter... what you are promised is surely true.﴾ The beginning and end of this surah correspond, since at its beginning He said, ﴿What you are promised is surely true,﴾ and at its end He said, ﴿So woe to those who disbelieve from their Day which they are promised.﴾ Regarding the explanation of these verses, there are several issues:

**The first issue:** We have already mentioned the wisdom behind oaths. It is one of the noble topics and great subjects, in the commentary on Surah al-Saffat. We repeat it here, and it has several aspects:

The first: the disbelievers sometimes acknowledged that the Prophet ﷺ was dominant in establishing proof, but they attributed this to argumentativeness, claiming that he knew within himself the falsity of what he said, and that he overcame us through the power of disputation rather than the truth of his speech. This is like how some people, when their opponent establishes a proof against them and they have no argument left, say: "He defeated me because of his knowledge of the methods of debate and my inability in that regard," while they know within themselves that the truth is in their hand. So the speaker who gives proof has no way left except the oath, so he says: "By God, the matter is as I say, and I do not argue with you in falsehood." This is because if he took another path, by presenting another proof, then when that other proof was complete, the opponent would say about it what he said about the first, that it was a demonstration of the power of debating skill. Nothing would remain except silence, or clinging to oaths and abandoning the establishment of proof.

The second: the Arabs used to avoid false oaths and believed that they left dwellings desolate. The Prophet ﷺ swore often by every noble thing, and this did not increase him except in elevation and steadfastness. They had knowledge that he did not swear by them falsely, for otherwise the ill omen of oaths would have struck him, and he would have suffered harm at some time.

The third: all the oaths by which Allah the Exalted swore are proofs that He presented in the form of oaths. An example of this is the statement of someone to his benefactor: "By the right of your many blessings, I will never cease to thank you." He mentions the blessings, which are a cause that makes thanks continue, and takes the path of an oath. Likewise, all these things are a proof of Allah the Exalted's power to restore. If it is asked: "Why did He present them in the form of oaths?" We say: because when a speaker begins his speech with an oath, the listener knows that he intends to speak a great word, so he listens more attentively than he would if he knew the speech was of no consequence. So he began with the oath and inserted the proof in the form of an oath until the people turned to listen to it. Thus the clear demonstration and the firm explanation came to them in the form of an oath. We have fully discussed this in the commentary on Surah al-Saffat.

**The second issue:** In all the surahs in which Allah swore at their beginning without letters, the oath was to establish one of the three foundations: the oneness of God (tawhid), the prophethood (risalah), and the gathering (hashr). These are the foundations by which faith is completed. Allah did not swear to establish tawhid except in one surah of those surahs, which is ﴿By those arrayed in ranks﴾ [al-Saffat: 1], where He said within it: ﴿Indeed, your God is surely One﴾ [al-Saffat: 4]. This is because, although they said, ﴿Has he made the gods one God?﴾ [Sad: 5] as a denial, and they exaggerated in polytheism, yet within the folds of their statements and the variations of their conditions they would express tawhid, and they used to say: ﴿We do not worship them except that they bring us near to Allah in position﴾ [al-Zumar: 3], and Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, "Allah."﴾ [Luqman: 25]. So they did not truly exaggerate in denying the first matter sought, and He sufficed with proof and did not multiply oaths.

In two of these surahs He swore to establish the truthfulness of Muhammad ﷺ and that he was a messenger: in one with a single matter, which is His saying: ﴿By the star when it sets, your companion has not strayed﴾ [al-Najm: 1-2]; and in the second with two matters, which is His saying: ﴿By the morning brightness, and by the night when it covers, your Lord has not forsaken you, nor has He detested you﴾ [al-Duha: 1-3]. This is because the oath to establish his prophethood has been frequent with letters and the Qur'an, as in His saying: ﴿Ya-Sin. By the wise Qur'an, indeed you are among the messengers﴾ [Ya-Sin: 1-3]. We have already mentioned the ruling on this: the miracle of the Prophet ﷺ is the Qur'an, so He swore by it so that the reference in the oath would be to the proof. In the remaining surahs, what was sworn to was the gathering, the recompense, and what is connected to them, because their denial of these was beyond all limits, and the oath with letters did not cover it.

**The third issue:** Allah the Exalted swore by the feminine sound plurals in five surahs, and He did not swear by a masculine sound plural in any surah at all. So He did not say "by the righteous of My servants," nor "by those brought near," and so on. Yet the masculine is more noble. This is because the sound plurals with waw and nun are usually for those who have intellect. We have mentioned that swearing by these things is not for explaining tawhid except in the case where the matter becomes apparent in it and they acknowledge it, nor for prophethood, since that is achieved in the forms of the oath by letters and the Qur'an.

What remains is that the intended purpose is to establish the gathering and recompense. But the establishment of the gathering is for the reward of the righteous and the punishment of the wicked, and the benefit of that returns to those who have intellect. So the matter required that the oath be by others. And Allah knows best.

**The fourth issue:** In the surah in which He swore to establish tawhid, He began by swearing by the stationary things, saying: ﴿By those arrayed in ranks﴾ [al-Saffat: 1]. In the remaining four surahs He swore by moving things. He said: ﴿By the winds that scatter﴾, and said: ﴿By those sent forth﴾ [al-Mursalat: 1], and said: ﴿By those who drag forth﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 1]. This is supported by His saying: ﴿By those who glide... then those who outstrip﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 3-4], and He said: ﴿By the charging ones﴾ [al-Adiyat: 1]. This is because the gathering involves joining and separating, and that is more fitting with motion. Or we may say that in all four surahs He swore by the winds, as explained, which gather and scatter. The one who is able to bring together scattered clouds by the scattering and sending winds is able to bring together scattered parts by whatever means He chooses by His will, the Exalted.

**The fifth issue:** Regarding "those that scatter" (al-dhariyat), there are several opinions:

The first: they are the winds that scatter dust and other things, as the Exalted said: ﴿which the winds scatter﴾ [al-Kahf: 45].

The second: they are the stars, from *dhara* (to scatter), meaning to move quickly.

The third: they are the angels.

The fourth: it is the Lord of the scatterers. The first opinion is the most sound.

**The sixth issue:** The four matters may be four distinct matters, and they may also be one matter having four aspects:

The first: it is what has been narrated from Ali (peace be upon him), that the scatterers are the winds, the carriers are the clouds, the runners are the ships, and the distributors are the angels who distribute provisions.

The second, which is the closest: these are four attributes of the winds. The scatterers are the winds that first produce the clouds. The carriers are the winds that carry the clouds, which are vapour of water, and when they pour, great torrents flow. They are loads heavier than mountains. The runners are the winds that move the clouds after carrying them. The distributors are the winds that spread the rains over the regions. It may be said that these are four matters mentioned in correspondence with four other matters by which the restoration is completed. This is because the parts that have been scattered, some of them lie in the depths of the earths, some in the depths of the seas, and some in the atmosphere of the air, and these are the subtle vaporous parts that separate from bodies. So His saying: ﴿By the scatterers﴾ means that which gathers the scattered things from the earth, since the scatterer is what scatters dust from the surface of the earth. His saying: ﴿those that carry a heavy load﴾ refers to what gathers parts from the atmosphere and carries them as a load, for the wind does not lift dust as a load, rather it moves it from one place and throws it in another, unlike clouds, for it carries it and moves it through the atmosphere as a load from which nothing falls. His saying: ﴿those that run with ease﴾ is a reference to what gathers water, for whoever makes heavy ships run through the currents of the seas to the shores is able to move parts from the sea to the land. When it becomes clear that gathering from the earth, the atmosphere of the air, and the midst of the seas is possible, and when it is gathered, there remains the breathing of the spirit, but the spirit is by the command of Allah, as He said: ﴿They ask you about the soul. Say: the soul is of the command of my Lord﴾ [al-Isra': 85]. Then He said: ﴿those that distribute by command﴾: the angels who breathe the spirit into the body by the command of Allah. He mentioned them as "distributors" because human beings do not differ in their bodily parts in any clear way: everyone has a head and feet, and people are close in number and measure. But the great difference is in souls, for the noble and the base are at the furthest extremes of difference. That unequal division is distributed by a chooser who distributes and a commanded one who chooses. So He said: ﴿those that distribute by command﴾.

**The seventh issue:** What is the grammatical status of these accusatives? As for ﴿ذَرْوًا﴾ (dharwan), there is no doubt that it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar). As for ﴿وِقْرًا﴾ (wiqran), it is an object (maf'ul bihi), as one says: "So-and-so carried a heavy load (adlan thaqilan)." It may also be a noun placed in the position of the verbal noun, as one says: "He struck him with a whip (sawtan)," supported by the reading of the one who read it with a fatha on the waw. As for ﴿يُسْرًا﴾ (yusran), it is also in the accusative, being an adjective of a verbal noun, its implied sense being "running with ease." As for ﴿فالمُقَسِّماتِ أمْرًا﴾ (al-muqassimati amran), it is either an object, as one says: "So-and-so distributed the provision or the wealth," or it is a circumstantial state (hal) that came in the form of a verbal noun, as one says: "I killed him patiently (sabran)," meaning he was made to endure. Likewise here: ﴿those that distribute by command﴾, meaning commanded.

If it is asked: if ﴿وِقْرًا﴾ is its object, why is it not plural, and why was it not said: "those that carry heavy loads (awqaran)"? We say: because the carriers, as we have explained, are attributes of the winds, and they follow one load. For a wind blows and drives the cloud so that it overtakes the cloud, then another wind blows and drives it, and sometimes it turns away from it to the right and left because of the differing winds. The same applies to "those that distribute by command" when we say it is an object, because a group who are commanded distributes one command. Or we may say it is in the sense of repetition, as if He had said: "those that carry a load, a load, and those that distribute a command, a command."

**The eighth issue:** What is the benefit of the particle *fa'* (then)? We say: if we say these are attributes of the winds, then it indicates the order of matters in existence, for the scatterers produce the clouds, and then they distribute the rains over the regions. If we say they are four matters, then the *fa'* indicates order in the oath, not order in what is sworn by. It is as if He said: "I swear by the scattering winds, then by the carrying clouds, then by the running ships, then by the distributing angels." His saying ﴿فالحامِلاتِ﴾ (then the carriers) and His saying ﴿فالجارِياتِ﴾ (then the runners) indicate the explanation of the benefits in the winds: on land, the producing of clouds, and at sea, the running of ships. Then ﴿المُقَسِّماتُ﴾ (the distributors) indicates what results from the carrying of clouds and the running of ships, namely provisions and profits that come by the division of Allah the Exalted. So the ships of some people run as they desire and make no profit, while others profit without being aware of it, as He the Exalted said: ﴿It is We who apportioned among them their livelihood﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 32].

The first: ﴿By the sky having paths﴾. It has been said that al-hubuk means the paths (al-tara'iq). On this view, it is possible that what is meant is the paths and courses of the stars, as is said of the (ornamented) roads (al-mahabik). It is also possible that what is meant is the shapes in the sky caused by the stars: in the direction of its stars there is the path of the Dragon (al-tinnin), the Scorpion (al-'aqrab), the Eagle (al-nasr), which the astrologers (ashab al-suwar) speak of, the Zodiac belt of Gemini (manṭaqat al-jawza'), and other things like paths. On this view, what is meant is the sky adorned with the adornment of the stars, and similar to it is His saying: ﴿By the sky of the constellations﴾ [al-Buruj: 1]. It has also been said that its hubuk is its solidity (sifaquha); it is said of a thick garment that it has good hubuk. On this view it is like His saying: ﴿By the sky of the return﴾ [al-Tariq: 11], because of its strength and power. This is what has been said about it.

The second discussion: concerning what is sworn to, which is His saying: ﴿Indeed you are in a discordant saying﴾. Regarding its interpretation there are various views, all of which are sound.

The first: ﴿Indeed you are in a discordant saying﴾, concerning Muhammad (ﷺ): at one time you say he is trustworthy, and at another time you say he is a liar; at one time you attribute madness to him, and at another time you say he is a soothsayer, a poet and a sorcerer. This is possible, but it is weak, since there is no need for an oath on this view, because they used to say that without denial, so that it would need to be emphasised with an oath.

The second: ﴿Indeed you are in a discordant saying﴾, meaning: not steadfast upon one matter. Whoever does not hold firm to one saying is not certain in his belief, so it is as if He said: "By the sky, indeed you are not resolute in your beliefs, and you only display resolution out of your intense obstinacy." On this view there is a benefit: when they said to the Prophet (ﷺ), "You know that you are not truthful in what you say, and you are only disputing, and we are unable to contend with argument," He said: ﴿By those that scatter dust, scattering﴾, meaning: you are truthful and not obstinate. Then He said: "Rather, by Allah, you are certain that I am truthful," thus reversing the matter upon them.

The third: ﴿Indeed you are in a discordant saying﴾, meaning contradictory. As for the Resurrection, you say there is no resurrection and no life after death, then you say: "We found our fathers following a community." If there is no life after death and the dead have no awareness, what harm would come to your fathers if you opposed them? This would only be valid from those who say that after death there is punishment; yet if we knew something the dead would dislike, it would be shown. So there is no sense in your saying, "We do not attribute our fathers to error after their death." And how, when you tie your mounts at the graves of the great? As for Tawhid, you say the Creator of the heavens and the earth is Allah, exalted, and none other, then you say He is the God of the gods, and you return to association. As for the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), you say he is a madman, then you say to him, "You overcome us by the strength of your argument." How can a madman be capable of coherent, inimitable speech? And other contradictory matters.

Then He said, Exalted is He: ﴿Killed are the conjecturers (al-kharrasun)﴾. This indicates that what is meant by His saying ﴿in a divergent speech﴾ is that they are not steadfast in any matter and not certain, but rather they guess and conjecture. Its meaning is: ﴿Cursed are the conjecturers﴾, a supplication against them with something disliked. Then He described them, saying: ﴿who are in heedlessness, inattentive﴾. In this there are two issues, one verbal and the other semantic.

As for the verbal issue: His saying ﴿inattentive (sahun)﴾ may be a predicate after a predicate, with the subject being His saying ﴿they (hum)﴾, and the implied meaning is: they are in heedlessness, inattentive, just as one says "Zayd is ignorant, oppressive," not intending to describe the ignorant person by the oppressive, but rather to inform about Zayd with both attributes. It may also be that ﴿inattentive﴾ is the predicate and ﴿in heedlessness﴾ is an adverbial complement of it, just as one says "Zayd is seated in his house"; the predicate is "seated" alone, and "in his house" explains the place of sitting. Likewise, ﴿in heedlessness﴾ explains the place of the heedlessness, which makes it valid to describe a definite noun by a sentence; were it not for this, describing a definite noun by a sentence would not be permissible.

As for the semantic issue: describing the conjecturer with heedlessness and immersion in falsehood establishes that the conjecturer is a term of blame. This is because what has no path to it except conjecture, when one conjectures and the conjecturer is so called, does not imply deficiency, as one says of the conjecturers of fruits, of armies, and other things. But conjecturing in the place of knowledge and certainty is blameworthy, so He said: ﴿Killed are the conjecturers﴾, ﴿who are﴾ ignorant and heedless, not those whose way is defined as estimation and guessing. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿inattentive﴾ after ﴿in heedlessness﴾ indicates that they have fallen into ignorance and falsehood, and have forgotten themselves therein, so they have not returned from it. Then He, Exalted is He, said:

﴿They ask: when is the Day of Judgment?﴾ If it is said: time is made the adverbial container of actions, and it is not possible for time to be the container of another container; yet here "ayyana" (أيّانَ) is made the container of the day, saying ﴿when is the Day of Judgment﴾, and one says "when does Zayd arrive," and it is answered "on Friday," and one does not say "when is Friday." This, from them, is a response to His saying ﴿and indeed the Religion will surely come to pass﴾, as if they said: when will it happen? as mockery. And the omission of the one asked about in His saying ﴿They ask﴾, where He did not say "they ask whom," indicates that their aim is not the answer, but that they ask in mockery.

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿On the Day they will be tried upon the Fire﴾ may bear two meanings.

The first: that it is an answer to their saying, ﴿When will it occur?﴾ In that case, just as they did not ask as one seeking knowledge, so He did not answer them with the answer of one who informs and clarifies, when He said: ﴿On the Day they will be tried upon the Fire﴾. This is like someone who says, "How long will you promise my enemies and break your promise? Both statements are in the form of a question and an answer, yet the first does not intend a question, and the second does not intend an answer. If it is said, "This leads to an implied omission (idmar)," we say that the omission is unavoidable, because His words, ﴿Taste your trial﴾, are not connected to what precedes them except by an omission, meaning: "and they will be tried." It has been said that its meaning is "they will be burned." The better view is that its meaning is "they will be presented to the Fire as gold is presented to the Fire by one testing it." The word ʿalā (upon) suits this meaning. If the intended meaning were "they will be burned," then bi-l-nār (with the Fire) or fī l-nār (in the Fire) would be more fitting, because fitnah is testing. As for what is said about "one who tested him," and about "the testing of stones," that refers to the meaning of the verbal noun of fitan (trials). Here He said, ﴿Taste your trial﴾, and fitnah is examination. We say: it is possible that what is meant is that you used to seek it hastily through explicit speech, as in His words quoting them: ﴿Our Lord, hasten for us our share before the Day of Reckoning﴾ [Ṣād: 16], and His words, ﴿Then bring us what you promise us﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 70], and so on. What indicates this here is His words: ﴿They ask, "When is the Day of Judgment?"﴾, for this is a kind of hastening. It is also possible that what is meant is hastening in action, which is persisting in obstinacy and displaying corruption, for that hastens the punishment.

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿On the Day they will be tried upon the Fire﴾ may bear two meanings.

The first: that it is an answer to their saying, ﴿When will it occur?﴾ In that case, just as they did not ask as one seeking knowledge, so He did not answer them with the answer of one who informs and clarifies, when He said: ﴿On the Day they will be tried upon the Fire﴾. Their ignorance of the second matter is stronger than their ignorance of the first, and it is not permissible for the answer to be more obscure than the question. If someone says, "When will Zayd arrive?" and the answerer says, "On the day his companion arrives," while the day of the companion's arrival is not known, this answer is not valid unless the speech is in the form of an answer and is not truly an answer. This is like someone who says, "How long will you promise my enemies and break your promise? Until when will this breaking of promises go on?" and the other becomes angry and says, "Until the most ill-omened day for you." Both statements are in the form of a question and an answer, yet the first does not intend a question, and the second does not intend an answer. Likewise here: He said, ﴿On the Day they will be tried upon the Fire﴾, as a response to their mockery with a threat, not in order to give a clarification.

The second: that this is the beginning of a statement whose completion is in His words, ﴿Taste your trial﴾. If it is said, "This leads to an implied omission (idmar)," we say that the omission is unavoidable, because His words, ﴿Taste your trial﴾, are not connected to what precedes them except by an omission, meaning: "and they will be tried." It has been said that its meaning is "they will be burned." The better view is that its meaning is "they will be presented to the Fire as gold is presented to the Fire by one testing it." The word ʿalā (upon) suits this meaning. If the intended meaning were "they will be burned," then bi-l-nār (with the Fire) or fī l-nār (in the Fire) would be more fitting, because fitnah is testing. As for what is said about "one who tested him," and about "the testing of stones," that refers to the meaning of the verbal noun of fitan (trials). Here He said, ﴿Taste your trial﴾, and fitnah is examination. If it is said: if you make ﴿On the Day they will be tried upon the Fire﴾ a statement addressed to them, ﴿Taste your trial﴾, then what is His words, ﴿This is what you used to seek to hasten﴾?

We say: it is possible that what is meant is that you used to seek it hastily through explicit speech, as in His words quoting them: ﴿Our Lord, hasten for us our share before the Day of Reckoning﴾ [Ṣād: 16], and His words, ﴿Then bring us what you promise us﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 70], and so on. What indicates this here is His words: ﴿They ask, "When is the Day of Judgment?"﴾, for this is a kind of hastening. It is also possible that what is meant is hastening in action, which is persisting in obstinacy and displaying corruption, for that hastens the punishment.

Page 172

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in gardens and springs﴾. After describing the state of the deceivers and the criminals, He described the state of the righteous, God-fearing person. On this verse there are several issues.

**The first issue:** We have mentioned that the God-fearing person has levels. The lowest of them is to guard against shirk (associating partners with God), and the highest is to guard against anything other than God. The lowest rank of the God-fearing is the Garden (Jannah). So every accountable person who avoids disbelief will enter the Garden and be provided with its bliss.

**The second issue:** Sometimes the Garden is mentioned in the singular, as in God's words: ﴿The likeness of the Garden which the God-fearing have been promised﴾ (Muhammad 47:15). Sometimes it is mentioned in the plural, as in this place, where He says: ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing are in gardens﴾. Sometimes it is mentioned in the dual, as He says: ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾ (al-Rahman 55:46). What is the wisdom in this? We say: as for the singular, in the context of promise, it is because the dwellings, trees and rivers are joined together and so form one garden. As for the wisdom of the plural, it is because in comparison with this world, and in relation to its own gardens, they are gardens that no number can enumerate. As for the dual, we will mention it in the chapter of al-Rahman; however, we say here: God, when speaking of the promise, used the singular for the Garden, and likewise when speaking of the purchase, where He said: ﴿Indeed, God has purchased from the believers their lives and their wealth in exchange for that they will have the Garden﴾ (al-Tawbah 9:111). When speaking of the giving, He used the plural, indicating that there is an increase in what is promised. The point of contention would be if He promised gardens and then said that they are in one garden, because that would be less than what was promised.

**The third issue:** His words ﴿and springs﴾ require that the God-fearing person be within them. There is no pleasure in a person being in water or any other liquid. We say its meaning is "amid the springs," that is, between the rivers, as evidenced by the fact that His words ﴿in gardens﴾ mean nothing other than "between gardens and among them," because the Garden is the trees, and he must be between them. The same applies to the springs. The indefiniteness of the word, although it is definite in meaning, is for magnification, as one says: "So-and-so is a man," meaning great in manhood.

As for His words ﴿taking what their Lord has given them﴾, there are issues and subtleties in it. As for the issues:

The first of them: What is the meaning of ākhidhīna (taking)? We say there are two views on it:

One: receiving what He has given them little by little, without fully taking possession of it all at once, because it is impossible to take possession of what has no end.

Second: taking, meaning accepting with the acceptance of one who is pleased, as He said: ﴿and He takes the charities﴾ (al-Tawbah 9:104), that is, He accepts them. This was mentioned by al-Zamakhshari. There is also a third view: His words ﴿in gardens﴾ indicate dwelling only, while His words ﴿taking﴾ indicate ownership. That is why one says "he took the land of such-and-such" or "the fortress of such-and-such" when he enters it as its owner. Likewise, one says of someone who bought a house or an orchard that he took it for a small price, meaning he owned it, even if there was no physical seizing or acceptance with pleasure. In that case, the benefit is to show that their entry into it is not the entry of a borrower or a loan that can be reclaimed from him, but rather it is their possession, which they bought with their wealth and themselves from God, exalted is He. His words ﴿He has given them﴾ serve to show that their taking of it was not by force or conquest, but was by God's giving, exalted is He. In this view, the word ﴿mā﴾ refers to the Gardens and the springs.

[p. 173]

And His words ﴿Indeed, they were before that doers of good﴾ are an indication of its price, meaning they took it and owned it through good-doing, as He said: ﴿For those who have done good is the best (reward)﴾ (Yunus 10:26), with the preposition of ownership (lām al-milk), and that is the Garden.

**The second issue:** ākhidhīna (taking) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and it has the meaning of the saying "they take." Why did He say ﴿mā ātāhum﴾ (what He has given them) and not ﴿mā yu'tīhim﴾ (what He gives them), so that the two words agree and the meaning fits? Because His words ﴿ātāhum﴾ (He has given them) indicate something finished in the past, while ﴿yu'tīhim﴾ (He gives them) (an-Nisa 4:152) indicates continuity. The giving of God in the Garden is renewed every day and has no end. Especially if we interpret taking as accepting: how is it correct to say "so-and-so accepts today what Zayd gave him yesterday"? We say: according to the interpretation we have mentioned, there is no problem, because its meaning is that they come to own what He has given them. The giving may occur yesterday and the owning today. As for what they have mentioned, we say: God gave the believer the Garden while he was in this world, except that he had not yet picked its fruits. So he enters it in the state of one who takes, and perhaps he takes something better than what was given to him. This does not contradict his entering it in that state, just as one says: "I came to you frightened, and then I became secure." What you have mentioned would only be a problem if their taking were limited to what was given to them before. That is not the case. Rather, they entered it on that basis and did not think of anything else, so God gives them what did not occur to them, and they take what God gives them, even though they entered it in order to take what He had given them. His words, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, the companions of the Garden today are busy with joy﴾ (Ya-Sin 36:55) refer to their taking what He has given them, which we have discussed in the chapter of Ya-Sin.

**The third issue:** To what does ﴿dhālika﴾ (that) refer? We say it has two possibilities:

One: before their entry, because His words ﴿in gardens﴾ carry the meaning of entering, meaning: before they entered the Garden, they did good.

The second: before God gave them what He gave them, the best (reward), which is the Garden, and then they took it. There are other views too, namely that ﴿dhālika﴾ refers to the Day of Judgment, which has already been mentioned.

**As for the subtleties:** some have already been mentioned. Among them: when He said ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing﴾, since it refers to guarding against shirk, it is as if He had said "those who believe." But faith together with righteous deeds yields two felicities, and for this reason it is a stronger indication than the saying "they did good."

**The second subtlety:** As for God-fearing (taqwa), it is because when one says "There is no god but God," he has guarded against shirk. As for doing good (iḥsān), it is because when he says "except God," he has performed good. For this reason it has been said regarding the meaning of the word of taqwa that it is "There is no god but God." And regarding iḥsān He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And who is better in speech than one who invites to God﴾ (Fussilat 41:33). It has also been said in the interpretation of ﴿Is the reward of good anything but good?﴾ (al-Rahman 55:60) that iḥsān is the bringing of the statement "There is no god but God." At that point the two do not separate; rather, they are mutually inseparable.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 51, verse 17:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They used to sleep but little of the night﴾, serves as an explanation of their being doers of good (muhsinin). It is like saying: "Hatim was generous; he would give away what he possessed and would not withhold his utmost effort." There are several points concerning it:

The first: "qalilan" (little) is in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarf), its implied sense being "they used to sleep little." You say "qama ba'da al-layl" (he stood for part of the night), so "ba'da" is put in the accusative as an adverb of time. The predicate of kana (was) is His saying "yahja'un" (they sleep), and "ma" is redundant (za'ida). This is the well-known view. There is another view, namely that one says "kanu qalilan" means the negation of sleep from them. This is transmitted from al-Dahhak and Muqatil. Al-Zamakhshari rejected that "ma" is negative and said: "It is not permissible for it to be negative, because what follows 'ma' does not govern what precedes it; you do not say 'Zaydan ma darabtu' (Zayd, I did not strike). Yet what follows 'lam' may govern what precedes it, as in 'Zaydan lam adrib' (Zayd, I did not strike)." The reason for this is that a transitive verb acts in negation by analogy with affirmation, for when you say "darab Zayd 'Amran" (Zayd struck 'Amr), the connection of his action to 'Amr is established. When you say "ma darabahu" (he did not strike him), no action has occurred from him that would be connected to him and transitive to him; but the negated is treated as the affirmed. Once this is established, negation in relation to affirmation is like the active participle in relation to the verb, for it works like the verb, but the active participle, when it carries the meaning of the past, does not govern: you do not say "Zayd darib 'Amran amsi" (Zayd is striking 'Amr yesterday). You say "Zayd darib 'Amran ghadan" (Zayd is striking 'Amr tomorrow), "al-yawm" (today), and "al-ana" (now), because the past no longer exists nor is its existence expected, so it is not connected to the object in reality. But the verb, owing to its strength, governs, while the active participle, owing to its weakness, does not. Knowing this, we say: "ma darab" is negation in the past, so negation and past tense combine in it and it is weakened. As for "lam adrib," although it turns the future into the past, the form is that of the future, so there is found in it what is found in the saying "Zayd darib 'Amran ghadan," and so it governs as an explanation of its meaning. However, the one who holds this view says that "qalilan" is not governed by His saying "yahja'un," but rather it is the predicate of kanu, meaning "they were few." Then He said: ﴿of the night, they used to sleep﴾, meaning they did not sleep at all, but rather kept vigil through the whole night. "Min" here is for specifying the kind (bayan al-jins), not for partitive meaning. This view, in that case, carries the sense of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿except those who believe and do righteous deeds, and few are they﴾ [Sad: 24]. This is because we have mentioned that His saying "innal-muttaqin" (indeed the God-fearing) carries the meaning of "those who believe," His saying "muhsinin" (doers of good) carries the meaning of "those who do righteous deeds," and His saying "kanu qalilan" carries the meaning of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and few are they﴾.

The second point: According to the well-known view that "ma" is redundant, "qalilan" may be an adjective of a verbal noun (masdar), its implied sense being "yahja'una huju'an qalilan" (they sleep a little sleep).

The third point: It is possible to say that "qalilan" is in the accusative as the predicate of kana, and "ma" is a verbal particle (masdariyya), its implied sense being "kana huju'uhum min al-layli qalilan" (their sleeping during the night was little). Thus the subject of "kanu" is the sleeping, and this is of the type of substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal), because their sleeping is connected to them, so it is as if He said "kana huju'uhum qalilan," just as one says "kana Zayd khuluquhu hasanan" (Zayd's character was good), and so there is no need to postulate an addition. Know that the grammarians do not call it a substitute in this case; they distinguish between the saying "Zayd hasan wajhuhu aw al-wajh" (Zayd, his face is good) and the saying "Zayd wajhuhu hasan" (Zayd, his face is good): in the first they say it is an adjective, and in the second a substitute. When we said it is of the type of substitution of inclusion, we meant it in a semantic sense, not as a technical term. Otherwise, "qalilan" when placed first has no equivalent in grammar as when it is placed last; so that your saying "Fulan qalil huju'uhu" (So-and-so, his sleeping is little) is not a substitute, while "Fulan huju'uhu qalil" is a substitute. On this basis, "ma" may be a relative pronoun (mawsula), meaning "kana ma yahja'una fihi qalilan min al-layl" (what they slept during was little of the night).

This is what relates to the wording. As for what relates to the meaning, we say: placing "qalilan" first in mention is not merely for the sake of rhyme (saj'), so that "yahja'un" and "yastaghfirun" fall at the ends of the verses; rather, it has two benefits.

The first: sleep is a rest for them, and the purpose is to explain their diligence and their enduring of wakefulness for God, Exalted is He. Had He said "kanu yahja'un," the first thing mentioned would have been their rest, and then He would describe it as little. A listener may overlook what follows the statement and think that their goodness and being doers of good is because they sleep. But when He placed His saying "qalilan" first, what comes first to understanding is the littleness of sleep. Whoever observes this benefit says "Fulan qalil al-huju'" (So-and-so sleeps little), and does not say "huju'uhu qalil" (his sleep is little), because the aim is to explain the littleness of sleep, not to explain sleep by the description of little or much. For if sleep did not exist, the negation of littleness would be more appropriate; and this is not so with the littleness of sleep, for if it did not exist, the apparent replacement for it would be abundance.

The second benefit: in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿of the night﴾. This is because little sleep during the day may be found in everyone, but the night is the time of sleep, and none keeps vigil in it in obedience except a devoted worshipper who turns to God. If it is said: "Sleeping occurs only at night; sleeping by day is not called huju'," we reply: mentioning the general matter and intending the specific is good, so we say "I saw an articulate, eloquent animal," whereas mentioning the specific and intending the general is good only in some contexts, so we do not say "I saw an eloquent, articulate animal." Knowing this, we say concerning His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They used to sleep little of the night﴾, that He mentioned a matter which is like the general, which may be followed by: "they used to glorify and seek forgiveness during the night," or "they used to stay awake," or other things. So when He said "yahja'un," it is as if He specified that general matter, which admits of that and of other things, so there is no difficulty in it.

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And at the dawns they seek forgiveness﴾. This indicates that they would perform the night prayer (tahajjud, voluntary prayer at night) and exert themselves, wishing that their deeds were more than that and purer, and they would seek forgiveness for their shortcomings. This is the conduct of the generous person, who brings the fullest forms of generosity and yet considers it little and apologises for his shortcoming. The stingy person brings little and considers it much, and reminds others of it as a favour.

There is another aspect to it, more subtle than this one. Since He, may He be exalted, had stated that they slept but little, and sleeping is a natural need, He said: ﴿they seek forgiveness﴾, that is, for that small amount of sleep. There is also another subtle point, serving as an answer to a question. He, may He be exalted, praised them for sleeping little, and did not praise them for staying awake much, nor did He say: "They used to stay awake much of the night." So what is the wisdom in this, given that staying awake is the effort and striving, not the sleeping? We say: it indicates that their sleep was itself a form of worship, since God praised them for sleeping little. That sleep led them to occupy themselves with another act of worship, namely seeking forgiveness at the time of the dawns, and it kept them from self-admiration and arrogance. There are also several discussions on this.

The first discussion concerns the particle bāʾ (ب). It is used here to express time, though it is not inherently a particle of time. Some grammarians (nuḥāh) have said: the particles of jarr (prepositions) may stand in place of one another. It is said regarding time: "I went out ten days before the end (of the month)," "I went out by night," and "in the month of Ramadan." So lām (ل), bāʾ (ب) and fī (في) are used interchangeably. The same applies to place: one says "aqamtu bi-l-madīnati kadhā" and "aqamtu fīhā" (I stayed in the city such-and-such), and "ra'aytuhu bi-baldati kadhā" and "ra'aytuhu fīhā" (I saw him in such-and-such town).

If it is asked: what is the verification of this? We say: particles have different meanings, just as nouns and verbs do. However, particles are not independent in conveying meaning, whereas nouns and verbs are independent. Yet among some particles there is divergence and distance, as there is among nouns and verbs: "bayt" (house) and "maskan" (dwelling) differ and are not identical, and likewise "sakana" (he dwelt) and "makatha" (he remained). This is not the case for every two nouns that may be imagined, or every two verbs that may exist.

Knowing this, we say: between bāʾ, lām and fī there is a shared element. As for bāʾ, it denotes adhesion (ilṣāq), and one who is in a place is adhered to it and connected to it. Likewise, with respect to time, a verb: if one says "sāra bi-l-nahār" (he travelled by day), its meaning is that he went in a manner connected with the day. Similarly, God's words ﴿and at the dawns they seek forgiveness﴾ mean: seeking forgiveness connected with the dawns and conjoined with them, because whatever exists in something is conjoined with it.

If it is asked: is there a difference in meaning between them? We say: yes. This is because whoever says "I stood (in prayer) by night" and "I seek forgiveness by the dawns" reports two things, and this is more indicative of the act occurring with the very first part of the time than saying "qumtu fī al-layl" (I stood in the night). The reason is that the latter demands that time encompass the act. Likewise, the saying "aqamtu bi-baldati kadhā" (I stayed by such-and-such town) does not indicate that he was surrounded by the town, whereas "aqamtu fīhā" (I stayed in it) indicates that it encompassed him. So the saying "aqamtu bi-l-baldati" and "da'awtu bi-l-asḥār" is more general than "qumtu fīhi," because one who stands in a thing stands by it, but one who stands by a thing is not necessarily standing in it. Knowing this, God's words ﴿and at the dawns they seek forgiveness﴾ indicate that they never let a time pass without worship: at night they do not sleep, and at the first part of the pre-dawn they seek forgiveness. Thus it shows that they sought forgiveness without any sin having preceded it from them, because at the time of waking in the dawns the time had not been left free for sin.

If it is said: give more explanation, for some times are not made into adverbial expressions with bāʾ. One does not say "kharajtu bi-yawm al-jumʿa" (I went out by Friday), but one says "fī." We say: every act occurring in a time is connected to it. Going out on Friday is connected and conjoined with that time. But "kharajtu bi-yawm al-jumʿa" is not used. We say the difference between them is restriction (taqyīd) and absoluteness (iṭlāq). The proof is that if you say "kharajtu bi-nahārinā" (I went out by our day) or "bi-laylat al-jumʿa" (by Friday night), it is not good. But if you say "kharaja huwa bi-yawm saʿd" (he went out by the day of Saʿd), or "kharaja huwa bi-yawm naḥs" (he went out on an unlucky day), it is good. So day and night, since there is no particularity and restriction in them, the use of bāʾ with them is permissible. When you restrict and specify them, that permissibility disappears. Friday, since it has a particularity, does not permit the use of bāʾ. When the particularity is removed by indefiniteness, and you say "kharajtu bi-yawm kadhā" (I went out on such-and-such a day), the permissibility returns. The secret of this is that things like Friday, this hour, and that night contain something other than time, namely particularities. The particularity of a thing is in reality many matters, innumerable to the rational mind in detail, but limited in summary. An example: when you say "hādhā al-rajul" (this man), the general element in it is "the man." If you then say "al-rajul al-ṭawīl" (the tall man), he does not become specified, but he comes close to particularity and departs from the short ones. If you say "al-ʿālim" (the scholar), he does not become specified, but he departs from the ignorant. If you say "al-zāhid" (the ascetic), it is likewise. If you say "Ibn ʿAmr," he has departed from the sons of Zayd, Bakr, Khalid and others. When you say "hādhā," it encompasses all those specifications, which are not gathered together except in that one. So the time that is determined in it consists of matters other than time itself. The act is an event connected with a time, not arising from the time.

As for fī (في), it is correct, because whatever occurs in the general occurs in the specific, since the general is a matter contained within the specific. Fī applies to that in which a thing is. So it is correct to say "fī yawm al-jumʿa" (on Friday) and "fī hādhihi al-sāʿa" (at this hour).

As for the discussion of lām (ل), we will postpone it to its place, and some of it has already been mentioned in the commentary on God's words ﴿and the sun runs toward its resting place﴾ [Yā-Sīn: 38].

As for His words "hum" (they), it is not devoid of benefit. Al-Zamakhsharī said: its benefit is the restriction of those who seek forgiveness, that is, for their perfection in seeking forgiveness, as if others were not seekers of forgiveness, so they alone are the seekers of forgiveness. One says: "Fulān huwa al-ʿālim" (So-and-so is the scholar), for his perfection, as if he were unique in it. This is good. But there is another benefit to it: when God, may He be exalted, conjoined ﴿and at the dawns they seek forgiveness﴾ to His words ﴿they used to sleep but little of the night﴾, then if He had not emphasised the affirmation with the word "hum" (they), it would have been acceptable for its meaning to be: "and at the dawns they seldom seek forgiveness." One says: "Fulān qalīlan mā yu'dhī" (So-and-so seldom harms), and "ilā al-nās yuḥsin" (he is good to people). It may be understood that he rarely harms and rarely does good. But when you say "qalīlan mā yu'dhī wa-huwa yuḥsin" (he seldom harms, and yet he does good), that understanding is removed, and the meaning of his words "little harm, much good" appears in it.

Seeking forgiveness (istighfār) admits of several aspects.

The first: asking for forgiveness by speech, by their saying ﴿Our Lord, forgive us﴾ [al-Ḥashr: 10].

The second: asking for forgiveness by action, that is, at the dawns they perform another act seeking forgiveness, which is prayer or other acts of worship.

The third, which is the strangest of them, is that istighfār is from the pattern of "istaḥṣada al-zarʿu" (the crop became ripe for harvest), when the time for its harvest has come. So it is as if at the dawns they are deserving of forgiveness and the time of forgiveness comes to them. If it is said: then did God not delay their forgiveness until the pre-dawn? We say: at the time of pre-dawn the angels of the night and the day gather, and it is the witnessed time, so God says before a gathering of them: "Indeed I have forgiven My servant." The first is more apparent, and the second is more well known among the exegetes (mufassirūn).

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And in their wealth there is a right for the beggar and the deprived.﴾

We have mentioned repeatedly that Allah, after mentioning the glorification of Himself, mentions compassion toward His creation. And there is no doubt that one who sleeps little and seeks forgiveness at the hours before dawn has shown great glorification. So by His words ﴿And in their wealth there is a right﴾ He points to this. Concerning it there are several issues:

The first issue: He attributed the wealth to them. In other places He said: ﴿Spend from what Allah has provided you﴾ [Ya-Sin: 47], and He said: ﴿and from what We have provided them they spend﴾. We say: the reason for this is that in those places the mention was for urging, so He mentioned with it what removes the urging's obstacle and lifts the impediment, saying: it is the provision of Allah, and Allah provides for you, so do not fear poverty, and give. Here, however, He praised them for what they did, so there was no need for stinginess to be addressed.

The second issue: The well-known view regarding the "right" is that it is the measure known by the Shari'ah, and that is the zakat (obligatory almsgiving). In that case this would not be a description of praise, because a Muslim having a right in his wealth, which is zakat, is not a description of praise, since every Muslim is like that. Rather, as for the disbeliever, if we say he is addressed with the branches of Islam, then in his wealth there is a known right, except that when he embraces Islam it falls from him, and if he dies he is punished for leaving it; and if he pays it without Islam, it does not count in its place. So how is its being praise understood? We say the answer to this is from several aspects:

The first: We interpret "the beggar" as one who seeks by right, and "the deprived" as one who has no ability to ask and whom the Lawgiver has prevented from making a demand. Then the prevention may be because the seeker is not entitled, and it may be because the one asked has no remaining obligation, so he is not pressed. Allah the Exalted therefore said: in their wealth there is a right for the seeker, which is zakat, and for the one who does not seek, which is voluntary charity given. For that owner is not pressed for it, and the seeker is deprived of it, as a demand by way of tax (jizyah) and zakat; rather he asks by voluntary request. In that case it is as if He said: in their wealth there is zakat and charity, and charity from wealth is only by its being set aside, measured, and separated for the poor and the needy.

The second answer: His words ﴿And in their wealth there is a right for the beggar﴾ mean that their wealth is a container for their rights. The word "fi" (in) indicates containment, but a container is sought only for what is contained. So it is as if He said: they do not seek wealth nor gather it except that they make it a container for the right. Without doubt, what is sought from a container is what it contains, and the container is their wealth; so He made their wealth a container for the rights, and there is no praise beyond this. If it is said: would it have been more eloquent to say "their wealth is for the beggar"? We say: No, because one who has forty dinars and gives them in charity, his charity is not lasting; but if he strives, trades, lives for years, and pays zakat and charity, the amount paid is greater. This is like prayer and fasting: if someone weakens himself through them until he is unable to continue, he is not like one who moderates in them. To this refers the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "This religion is firm, so enter it gently, for the one who cuts through the ground has not left a land, nor preserved a back."

Regarding "the beggar and the deprived" there are several views:

One: the beggar is the one who speaks, that is the human being, and the deprived is every living creature other than him among the deprived animals. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "For every thirsty liver there is a reward."

The second, which is the most apparent and most well known: the beggar is the one who asks, and the deprived is the abstainer (mutaʿaffif) whom some people consider wealthy, so they give him nothing.

The first is like His words: ﴿Eat and graze your livestock﴾ [Ta-Ha: 54]. The second is like His words: ﴿And feed the contented and the one who asks﴾ [al-Hajj: 36]; so the contented one is like the deprived. If it is said that according to the first view the ordering is most excellent, since relieving the need of the speaker takes precedence over relieving the need of animals, then what is the ordering's rationale in the second view? We say there are two aspects:

One of them: the beggar's need is relieved before the deprived's need in existence, because his condition is known by his speech, and he asks due to the scarcity of his wealth, so he is given precedence in relieving his need; while the deprived is not known, so his need is not relieved except after becoming aware of him. Thus the mention is in the order that occurs.

The second: that this is an indication of the abundance of giving, so that one gives to the beggar, and if he does not find them, he himself asks about the needy, so he becomes both a seeker and one sought.

The third: that verbal eloquence is not abandoned in wise speech. The saying of one who says that their return is to us and their reckoning is upon us is not like His words: ﴿Indeed, to Us is their return﴾ ﴿Then indeed, upon Us is their reckoning﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 25–26]. Speech has a body, which is the wording, and a spirit, which is the meaning; and just as a person whose spirit has been illuminated with knowledge should illuminate his outward body with cleanliness, so too speech: many a wise word does not affect souls because its wording is weak. Knowing this, His words ﴿And at the hours before dawn they seek forgiveness﴾ ﴿And in their wealth there is a right for the beggar and the deprived﴾ are more eloquent in wording than our saying "and at the hours before dawn they seek forgiveness, and in their wealth there is a right for the deprived and the beggar." If it is said: the beggar was placed before the deprived here for the aspects you mentioned, why was the deprived placed before the beggar in His words ﴿the contented and the one who asks﴾ [al-Hajj: 36], since "the contented" is the one who does not ask and "the one who asks" is the beggar? We say: it has been said that "the contented" is the beggar and "the one who asks" is the one who does not ask, so there is no difference between the two passages. It has also been said that both "the contented" and "the one who asks" do not ask, but "the contented" does not expose himself and does not leave his house, while "the one who asks" exposes himself to taking by greeting and repeated visits, yet does not ask. It has also been said that "the contented" does not ask and "the one who asks" does ask. On this view, the meat of the sacrificed camel is distributed without a collector's demand or one entitled to a jizyah demand; whereas zakat has a claimant and a seeker, namely the collector and the imam. So His words ﴿for the beggar﴾ point to zakat, and His words ﴿and the deprived﴾, meaning the prevented, point to voluntary charity. Each is mentioned before the other, unlike the giving of meat.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And in the earth are signs for those who have certainty﴾, and this may bear two meanings:

The first: that it is connected to His words: ﴿Indeed, what you are promised is true﴾ and ﴿indeed, the Judgment is surely to occur﴾, and ﴿in the earth are signs for those who have certainty﴾, which show them that the Resurrection (al-hashr) is bound to happen, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And among His signs is that you see the earth humbled; but when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells. Indeed, He who has revived it is surely the Reviver of the dead﴾ [Fussilat: 39].

The second: that it is connected to the deeds of the God-fearing (al-muttaqun). For they feared God and magnified Him, and so they displayed compassion toward His servants. And for them there were signs in the earth and in themselves, through their attaining the truth in this matter. For whoever has in the earth wondrous signs has complete power, so he is feared and guarded against. And whoever has in people's selves profound wisdom and abundant blessings deserves to be worshipped, and sleep should be forsaken for his worship. When the servant sets worship against blessing, he finds his worship falling short of the due measure of thankfulness, so he seeks forgiveness for his shortcoming. And when he knows that provision comes from the sky, he does not withhold his wealth. The three following verses restate what preceded them. On this reading, God's words ﴿So by the Lord of the heaven and the earth﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 23] come as a return to the main discourse after the interjection, which makes the return stronger and clearer. There are several issues concerning this:

The first issue: How did He specify the certain (al-muqinin) as those for whom the signs exist, when the signs are present for everyone? God said: ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth which We have revived﴾ [Ya-Sin: 33]. We say: we have mentioned that the oath is the last thing the one presenting proof brings. This is because he first brings the proof; if it is accepted, that is well, and if it is not accepted, his opponent must attribute to him persistence in falsehood. For if the opponent is unable to refute it and does not accept it, he must acknowledge the strength of the argument, yet he attributes to him obstinacy, and so the path of the oath is fixed. Thus the signs of the earth did not benefit them, because the oath with His words ﴿By the scatterers, scattering﴾ indicated that clear proofs had already been established and signs mentioned, yet it did not benefit them. So He said within it: ﴿And in the earth are signs for those who have certainty﴾. Even if no benefit accrues to the stubborn obstinate person from them, the point stands. As for in Surat Ya-Sin and other places where He made the signs of the earth for the general public, no oath came there, nor was there a mention of signs before it. Therefore it is permissible to say that the earth contains signs for whoever contemplates it.

The second answer, which is the more correct, is that here the signs are, in fact and in consideration, for the believers: that is, these signs have actually come to them. And when He said "for everyone," its meaning is that there are signs in it for them if they look and reflect.

The second issue: Here He said ﴿And in the earth are signs﴾, and there He said ﴿And a sign for them is the earth﴾ [Ya-Sin: 33]. We say: when He made the sign "for those who have certainty," He used the plural form, because the one who has certainty never neglects God, exalted is He, in any state, and sees in every thing signs that point to Him. As for the heedless, he is not alerted except by many matters, so that the whole becomes to him like a single sign.

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿And in yourselves. Will you not see?﴾ This points to the proof from the self (al-dalil al-anfus). It is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We will show them Our signs on the horizons and within themselves﴾ [Fussilat: 53]. He chose from the proofs of the horizons what is on the earth, because it is manifest to those who stand upon it, for on its surfaces and its expanses are things whose kinds cannot be counted. The proof of the self in His saying ﴿And in yourselves﴾ is general, and it may be that it is specific to the believers. He used the form of address because it is more evident, since a person's knowledge of what is in himself is most complete. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And in yourselves﴾, may mean "and among you," as one says: "The stone in itself is hard," and by this is not meant the soul (nafs) which is the source of life, sensation and movement. It may also mean "and in your souls by which you live are signs." His saying ﴿Will you not see?﴾ in the interrogative form points to the clarity of these signs.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And in the heaven is your provision﴾ has several interpretations.

The first: in the clouds is the rain.

The second: ﴿And in the heaven is your provision﴾ means it is written (in the heaven).

The third: the decree of all provisions is from the heaven, and were it not for it, not a grain of sustenance would come into being on the earth. The three verses are arranged in a good order, because a person has matters which he needs and which must precede him so that he himself may come into existence; matters which accompany him in existence; and matters which come to him and exist after him so that he may remain by them. The earth is the place, and man needs it, and it must precede him, so He said: ﴿And on the earth are signs﴾. Then within the human self are matters of bodies and accidents, so He said: ﴿And in yourselves﴾. Then his survival is by provision, so He said: ﴿And in the heaven is your provision﴾. Were it not for the heaven, there would be no survival for people.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And what you are promised﴾ has several interpretations.

The first: the Garden which is promised, because it is in the heaven.

The second: it is from the (verb) al-i'ad (threatening/promising), because the passive form of awʿada, yuʿidu, is ﴿what you are promised﴾. That is, ﴿what you are promised﴾ is either from the Garden and the Fire, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Day they are over the Fire﴾ and His saying: ﴿Indeed the righteous are in gardens﴾, in which case it is a general promise; or it is from the punishment, in which case the address is with the disbelievers, and it is as if He, exalted is He, said: "And on the earth are signs for the certain (al-muqinin), sufficient. As for you, O disbelievers, in yourselves are signs which are the most evident of signs, and you deny them for the sake of the trash of this world and love of leadership. And in the heaven are provisions. So if you looked and reflected with the true reflection, you would not have abandoned the truth for the sake of provision, for it reaches you by every way; and you would have avoided falsehood, guarding against what you are promised of the descending punishment."

* * *

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿So by the Lord of the heaven and the earth, indeed it is truth, just as you speak﴾.

As for what is sworn to, there are several interpretations.

The first: ﴿what you are promised﴾, that is, what you are promised is truth, and His saying, exalted is He, supports this: ﴿Indeed what you are promised is surely true﴾. On this view, everything we have said about the interpretations of ﴿what you are promised﴾ returns (to this), if we say that it is the Garden, then what is sworn to is it.

The second: the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, that is, the Qur'an is truth, and what we mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿is turned away from it﴾ is evidence for this. On this view, His saying ﴿just as you speak﴾ means: it was spoken by the angel descending from Allah, just as you speak, and we will mention it.

The third: it refers to the religion (al-din), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed the religion is surely to occur﴾.

The fourth: it refers to the Day mentioned in His saying: ﴿When is the Day of Recompense?﴾ It is indicated by the description of the Day as truth in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is the true Day﴾ [An-Naba': 39].

The fifth: it refers to the statement which is said: ﴿This is what you used to seek to hasten﴾. [p. 180]

In the exegesis there are discussions:

The first: the fa' (particle "so") requires the sequence of one matter after another, so what is the earlier matter? We say there are two views:

One of them: the earlier proof. It is as if He, exalted is He, says: "Indeed what you are promised is true by a clear proof, then by oath and swearing."

The second: the earlier oath. It is as if He, exalted is He, says: "By the scattering ones (al-dhariyat)," then "So by the Lord of the heaven and the earth." On this view, the fa' is a conjunctive particle with which the particle of oath is repeated, just as the verb may be repeated, since it is correct to say: "And I passed by 'Amr." So His saying "By the scattering ones, scattering" and "the bearers of burdens" is a conjunction without repeating the particle of oath, while His saying "So by the Lord of the heaven" with the repetition of its particle. The reason for this is the occurrence of a separation between the two oaths. It may also be said that the earlier matter is the explanation of the reward in His saying: ﴿The Day they are over the Fire, they will be tried﴾ and His saying: ﴿Indeed the righteous are in gardens﴾. In this there is a benefit: the fa' serves as an alert that there is no need for an oath along with what has preceded of clear disclosure. So it is as if He says: "By the Lord of the heaven and the earth, indeed it is true," just as a speaker, after making his claim, says: "By God, the matter is as I have mentioned," confirming his statement with an oath, and indicating its affirmation without an oath.

The second discussion: He had earlier sworn by earthly matters, namely the winds, and by the heaven in His saying: ﴿By the heaven of the paths﴾, but He did not swear by its Lord. Here He swore by its Lord. We say: this is the same order. The speaker first swears by the lesser, and if it is not believed, he ascends to the greater. For this reason some people said: if someone says, "By your life, by God, he will not disbelieve," and if he says, "By God, by your life, there is no doubt he disbelieves," this is an argument. Even if the matter is contrary to what that speaker said, because disbelief is either in the heart, or by an explicit utterance concerning what is in the heart, or by an explicit act. What he mentioned is not explicit in magnifying the side of other than Allah. And it is strange about that speaker that he does not make the prior mention in the ordering (of limbs) indicative of sequence in ablution and other things.

The third discussion: it has been read as "mithlu" (in the nominative), and then it is an attribute of His saying "truly (laḥaqqun)". And mithlu, even though it is annexed to a definite noun, does not remove it from the permissibility of describing an indefinite noun with it. You say: "I saw a man like 'Amr," because it does not make it definite, since it is in the utmost indefiniteness. It has also been read as "mithla" (in the accusative), and it may have two possibilities:

One of them: that it is fatha-vowelled because it is annexed to what is weak; otherwise it would be permissible to say "Zayd is the killer of whoever knows him," or "the striker of whoever insults him."
