The fifth: it refers to the statement which is said: ﴿This is what you used to seek to hasten﴾. [p. 180]

In the exegesis there are discussions:

The first: the fa' (particle "so") requires the sequence of one matter after another, so what is the earlier matter? We say there are two views:

One of them: the earlier proof. It is as if He, exalted is He, says: "Indeed what you are promised is true by a clear proof, then by oath and swearing."

The second: the earlier oath. It is as if He, exalted is He, says: "By the scattering ones (al-dhariyat)," then "So by the Lord of the heaven and the earth." On this view, the fa' is a conjunctive particle with which the particle of oath is repeated, just as the verb may be repeated, since it is correct to say: "And I passed by 'Amr." So His saying "By the scattering ones, scattering" and "the bearers of burdens" is a conjunction without repeating the particle of oath, while His saying "So by the Lord of the heaven" with the repetition of its particle. The reason for this is the occurrence of a separation between the two oaths. It may also be said that the earlier matter is the explanation of the reward in His saying: ﴿The Day they are over the Fire, they will be tried﴾ and His saying: ﴿Indeed the righteous are in gardens﴾. In this there is a benefit: the fa' serves as an alert that there is no need for an oath along with what has preceded of clear disclosure. So it is as if He says: "By the Lord of the heaven and the earth, indeed it is true," just as a speaker, after making his claim, says: "By God, the matter is as I have mentioned," confirming his statement with an oath, and indicating its affirmation without an oath.

The second discussion: He had earlier sworn by earthly matters, namely the winds, and by the heaven in His saying: ﴿By the heaven of the paths﴾, but He did not swear by its Lord. Here He swore by its Lord. We say: this is the same order. The speaker first swears by the lesser, and if it is not believed, he ascends to the greater. For this reason some people said: if someone says, "By your life, by God, he will not disbelieve," and if he says, "By God, by your life, there is no doubt he disbelieves," this is an argument. Even if the matter is contrary to what that speaker said, because disbelief is either in the heart, or by an explicit utterance concerning what is in the heart, or by an explicit act. What he mentioned is not explicit in magnifying the side of other than Allah. And it is strange about that speaker that he does not make the prior mention in the ordering (of limbs) indicative of sequence in ablution and other things.

The third discussion: it has been read as "mithlu" (in the nominative), and then it is an attribute of His saying "truly (laḥaqqun)". And mithlu, even though it is annexed to a definite noun, does not remove it from the permissibility of describing an indefinite noun with it. You say: "I saw a man like 'Amr," because it does not make it definite, since it is in the utmost indefiniteness. It has also been read as "mithla" (in the accusative), and it may have two possibilities:

One of them: that it is fatha-vowelled because it is annexed to what is weak; otherwise it would be permissible to say "Zayd is the killer of whoever knows him," or "the striker of whoever insults him."

The second: that it is in the accusative as an explanation (al-bayan), its implied sense being "truly, a truth like," and it may be said that it is in the accusative as an attribute of an understood verbal noun (masdar), and its reasoning is that we have shown that what is meant by the pronoun in His saying ﴿indeed it (innahu)﴾ is the Qur'an, so it is as if He said: "Indeed the Qur'an is truth, spoken by the angel with a speaking like ﴿what you speak﴾," and "ma" is in the genitive, without doubt.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Has there reached you the story of the honoured guests of Abraham?﴾ This is an indication of consoling the heart of the Prophet ﷺ by showing that other prophets, peace be upon them, were like him in this. He chose Abraham because he was the elder of the messengers (shaykh al-mursalin), and because the Prophet ﷺ followed his way in some matters; and [it serves as] a warning to his people about what befell them from the guests, and from the raining of stones upon the sinful, misguiding wrongdoers. There are several issues in this:

The first issue: If the purpose is what you mentioned, consolation and warning, then what is the benefit in relating the account of the hospitality? We say: it is so as to be an indication of relief for the prophets, and of affliction for the ignorant and the foolish when it comes upon them from where they do not expect it. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Then Allah came upon them from where they did not expect﴾ [al-Hashr: 2]. Abraham, peace be upon him, had no knowledge of the descent of punishment, despite the elevation of his station.

The second issue: How did He call them "guests" when they were not? We say: when Abraham, peace be upon him, supposed them to be guests, Allah the Exalted did not contradict his supposition, out of honour for him. It is said in the words of the verifiers: the truthful one says what is, and the one who is truly sincere (ṣiddīq) says what will be.

The third issue: "Ḍayf" (guest) is a single word, and "al-mukramīn" (the honoured) is plural, so how did He describe the singular with the plural? We say: "al-ḍayf" applies to a group; one says "qawm ḍayf" (a guest people), and since it is a verbal noun (maṣdar), it is like the word "al-rizq" used as a maṣdar. He described them as "honoured" either because they are honoured servants, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Rather, they are honoured servants﴾ [al-Anbiya: 26], or because Abraham, peace be upon him, honoured them. If it is asked: with what did he honour them? We say: first, with a cheerful face; second, by seating them in the best and most graceful places; third, by hastening the hospitality; and after that, by urging the guest to eat and to sit. They were a number of angels: in one opinion three, Jibril, Mika'il and a third; in another opinion ten; and in another twelve.

The fourth issue: They were sent for punishment, as is evident from their saying: ﴿Indeed we have been sent to a criminal people﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 32]. They were not from the people of Abraham, peace be upon him; rather they were from the people of Lut. So what is the wisdom in their coming to Abraham, peace be upon him? We say: there is a profound wisdom in it, and its explanation is from two aspects:

One of them: Abraham, peace be upon him, was the elder of the messengers, and Lut was from his people. And it is part of the king's honour toward one who is under his charge and obedience that, when he sends a messenger to another, he tells him: "Pass by So-and-so the king, inform him of your message, and take his opinion on it."

And the second of them: when Allah the Exalted decreed to destroy a great people and a vast multitude, and this would grieve Abraham, peace be upon him, out of compassion for His servants, He told them: "Give him good news of a boy who will come forth from his loins, whose offspring will be many times those who are destroyed, and from whose loins the prophets, peace be upon them, will come forth."

ُThen God, exalted is He, said: ﴿When they entered upon him and said, "Peace." He said, "Peace, [you are] a people unknown."﴾ There are several issues concerning this verse:

**The first issue: What is the governing element (al-‘amil, the word that governs the case) of "idh" (when)?** There are several views.

The first: the governing element is what is implied by "al-mukramin" (the honored ones), if we say that God described them as honored because Abraham, peace be upon him, honored them. It is as if God were saying, "Be honored when they entered," for it is the nature of a generous man to honor his guest at the time of his entry.

The second: the governing element is what is implied by "al-day‘" (the guest), since we have said that "al-day‘" is a verbal noun (maṣdar). It is as if He were saying, "He hosted them when they entered."

The third: it is possible that the governing element is "atak" (has come to you), with the meaning: "The report of them has come to you at the time of their entering. So listen now to that," because "hal" (has) here is not truly interrogative but is for informing. This is preferable, because it is an explicitly stated verb. It is also possible to say, "Remember when they entered."

**The second issue: Why does the grammatical case (i‘rab) of the two words "salam" differ in the well-known recitation?** We first explain the aspects of the accusative (naṣb) and the nominative (raf‘), and then the aspects of the difference in case. As for the accusative, it may bear several aspects:

The first: that "salam" means the greeting, which is the best-known meaning. Its accusative is then as a verbal noun (maṣdar), the implied sense being "we greet with a greeting."

The second: that "salam" is a kind of speech by which the speaker is kept safe from either speaking in vain or sinning. Thus when they entered upon him and said "a good word" (salaman), they were kept safe from sin. In this case it is an object (maf‘ul) of the verb "qala" (said), because the object of "qala" is speech: one says "So-and-so said a speech" (qala kalaman). This is not like the construction "daraba-hu sawṭan" (he struck him with a whip), because the one struck there is not the whip, whereas here "qawl" is speech itself. This is explained by His words: ﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace."﴾ [al-Furqan: 63] and His words: ﴿Only the saying, "Peace, peace."﴾ [al-Waqi‘ah: 26].

The third: that it is the object of an omitted verb, the implied sense being "we convey to you a greeting" (nuballighuka salaman). It might be objected: if that were the meaning, he would have known that they were messengers of God at the greeting, so he would not have said "a people unknown," nor would he have brought food near to them, nor would he have felt apprehension. We answer: it is possible that they said, "We convey to you a greeting," without saying "from God, exalted is He," until Abraham, peace be upon him, asked them, "From whom are you conveying the greeting to me?" This is because a wise person does not bring a great matter except gradually. Since their awe was great, if they had added to it the great matter that is from God, exalted is He, Abraham, peace be upon him, would have been alarmed. Then Abraham, peace be upon him, busied himself with honoring them rather than asking them, and postponed the question until the time of leisure. Thus he regarded them as unknown between the greeting and the question about from whom the greeting came. This is the aspect of the accusative.

As for the nominative: we say it is possible that what is meant by "salam" is the greeting, which is also the best-known meaning. In that case it is a subject (mubtada’) whose predicate (khabar) is omitted, the implied sense being "Peace be upon you." The indefiniteness of the subject is allowed in the speech of one who says "Peace be upon you" just as one says "Woe to him." Or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, the implied sense being "his answer is peace." It is also possible that what is meant is a statement by which one gives greeting or indicates safety. Then it is the predicate of an omitted subject, the implied sense being "my affair is peace," meaning a parting of peace: there is no connection between me and you, for I do not know you. Or the subject may be "your statement," the implied sense being "your statement is peace, indicating safety, and you are a people unknown, so what is your business? For the matter has become unclear to me." This is what may be said regarding the accusative and the nominative.

As for the difference: on the well-known interpretation, namely that "salam" in both places means the greeting, we say the difference between them lies in terms of wording and in terms of meaning.

In terms of wording: "salamun ‘alayka" was permitted and found good because it is a subject that is indefinite, in that it is like what is left in its original state, since the original is that it should be accusative, implying "I greet you with a greeting," and "‘alayka" serves to specify who is intended by "salam." "‘Alayka" has no share of meaning other than that specifying, so it is like something outside the sentence. The complete sentence is "I greet with a greeting," just as you say "I struck Zayd on the roof": "on the roof" is outside the verb, the subject and the object, serving only to indicate location. When this is so, and greetings and supplications are very frequent, they changed from the verbal sentence to the nominal sentence and gave "‘alayka" a share in the sentence, saying "salamun ‘alayka." Thus "‘alayka" becomes for a necessary benefit, which is the predicative (khabariyyah) sense, and "salam" is left indefinite as it was in the accusative. Having understood this, the accusative is the original and the nominative is derived from it, and the original takes precedence over what is derived from it. So He said: ﴿They said, "Peace." He said, "Peace."﴾ The original was placed before what branches from it.

In terms of meaning: Abraham, peace be upon him, wanted to answer them with what is better, so he used the nominal sentence, for it indicates permanence and continuity more clearly. Our saying "Zayd sat" does not indicate this, because a verb must indicate renewal and occurrence. For this reason, if you say, "God exists now," the intellect would establish permanence, since it does not indicate renewal. But if someone said, "God came into existence now," a rational person would almost deny it, for the reason we have explained. So when they said "Peace," he replied "Peace be upon you," which is continuous and lasting.

As for our view that the intended meaning is "a statement that bears safety," the difference is clear: they uttered a statement bearing peace, and Abraham, peace be upon him, said to them: "Peace," that is, your statement bears peace, "and you are a people unknown," so the matter became confused for me.

If we say the intended meaning is a matter of peaceful parting and disengagement, and they greeted him by way of greeting, then there is a combination of two matters: the exaltation of the side of God and the care of the hearts of God's servants. For if he had said "Peace be upon you" while he did not know that they were among God's righteous servants, it would be possible that they were otherwise. Then the messenger would have granted them safety, for a greeting is a guarantee of safety, and the guarantee of a messenger is the guarantee of the sender. Thus he would be acting in the affair without God's permission, on God's behalf. So he said: "You have greeted me, and I am holding my affair in abeyance, a parting with no connection between us, until the situation becomes clear." This is indicated by God's words: ﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace."﴾ And in a similar sense He said to the Prophet ﷺ: ﴿So turn away from them and say, "Peace."﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 89], and He did not say "say peace" (qul salaman). That is because if the righteous persons mentioned in the Qur'an greeted the ignorant, this would not be a cause for the prohibition of confronting them. But if the Prophet ﷺ had greeted them, that would become a cause for the prohibition of confronting them. So He said, "Say, 'Peace,'" that is, my affair with you is a parting; we have left it until God's command comes with a command.

As for our view, in the sense of "we convey a greeting": when they said, "We convey to you a greeting," and Abraham, peace be upon him, did not know whether he was among those who said "Peace," the meaning is: if it is from God, then this greeting from Him has increased my honor by it; otherwise, a greeting has reached me from him, and by it is my honor, and I do not take pride in the greeting of another. This is what may be said regarding this, and God knows best what is meant. The first and second views are the ones to rely upon, for they are stronger, and both have been stated.

**The third issue:** In Surah Hud He said: ﴿When he saw their hands not reaching toward it, he regarded them with suspicion﴾ [Hud: 70], which indicates that their being unknown occurred after he had brought the calf near them. Here He says: ﴿He said, "Peace, [you are] a people unknown."﴾

[p. 182]

Then God, exalted is He, said:

﴿Then he turned quickly to his family and brought a fattened calf.﴾ ﴿He placed it before them and said, "Will you not eat?"﴾

The particle used is the *fa'* of sequence (*fa' al-ta'qib*, the *fa'* indicating that one thing follows immediately after another), which shows that he brought the food to them after they had shown disapproval. What is the explanation for this? We say: it is possible that some disapproval first arose in him from them, and then increased when they refrained from eating. What indicates this is that they had a form and appearance unlike that of ordinary people, and in themselves they seemed strange to everyone. Ibrahim (peace be upon him) and others shared in this impression. For this reason he did not say, "I disapprove of you," but said, ﴿"Indeed, you are a people unknown to us."﴾ (Al-Hijr 15:62), meaning: you seem strange to us, each of us finds you so. Then Ibrahim (peace be upon him) alone witnessed something from them, namely their refraining from eating, so he disapproved of them more than what was true of them in relation to everyone else. However, the account in Surat Hud is related in a fuller way than what is mentioned here. Here he did not specify the one who was given the good news, whereas there he named him, namely Ishaq. Here he did not say that the people were the people of whom, whereas there he said, "the people of Lut." In general, whoever reflects on the two surahs will know that the narrative is related there in a fuller manner, so it includes the additional point that is not mentioned here.

Let us return to explaining what he did of the manners of hospitality and what they did of the manners of being a guest. First, honoring a guest who has come to him, before they meet and before one of them greets the other, includes kinds of honor: a good welcome, going out to meet him, and preparing for him. Then the greeting from the guest in the good manner indicated by the accusative in His words, ﴿"Peace"﴾ (Adh-Dhariyat 51:25), either because it is emphasized by the verbal noun (*masdar*), or because it is a conveyance from one greater than him. Then the good reply indicated by the nominative (*raf'*), and the silence, does not contain fulfillment, for Ibrahim (peace be upon him) did not say, "Peace be upon you," but said, "A matter of peace," or "Your word is peace, but your peace is unfamiliar." For although that is detrimental to honor, yet an excuse is not the way of the noble, and the affection of God's enemies is not fitting for the prophets, peace be upon them. Then hastening the hospitality, indicated by His words, ﴿"Then he did not delay to bring"﴾ (Hud 11:69).

[p. 184]

And His words here, ﴿"he turned quickly"﴾, for *ruwagan* (turning aside quickly) indicates speed, and *al-rawgh* (turning aside), meaning a hidden glance or a hidden departure, is likewise. Then concealment: when the host brings something, he should keep it hidden from the guest, so that the guest does not prevent him from bringing it himself, since he turned away and did not say, "Bring it." The host's absence for a moment from the guest is considered commendable, so that the guest may rest and so that the host may bring what he needs, while the guest's modesty prevents him from [asking]. Then choosing the best, by His words, ﴿"fattened"﴾. Then bringing the food to them, not moving them to the food, by His words, ﴿"he placed it before them"﴾, because whoever brings food to a people, each one remains in his place, and the location does not vary for him. But if he moved them to where the food is, a difference in seating might arise there, so the one nearer would be brought closer and the one of higher rank would be crowded. Then the offer, not the command, since he said, ﴿"Will you not eat?"﴾ and did not say, "Eat." Then the host's being pleased by their eating, and not pleased by their leaving the food, as is found in some stingy, pretentious people who bring much food, and whose gaze and the gaze of the people of their household is fixed on the food, watching for when the guest will withdraw his hand from it. This is what indicates it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 51, verses 28–32:

Allah's words: ﴿So he felt a fear of them. They said, "Do not fear," and they gave him good news of a knowing boy.﴾ Then, the etiquette (adab) of the guest: when he eats, he observes the right of eating together (al-mu'akalah). This is shown by the fact that he (Ibrahim) feared them when they did not eat. Then, the obligation to state an excuse when refraining from eating is indicated by their words: ﴿Do not fear.﴾ Then, the good phrasing of the excuse. This is because whoever is abstaining from food, and food is brought before him, is in one of two situations.

The first: the food is not suitable for him, because it is harmful to him.

The second: he is too weak to digest that food. So the guest should not say, "This is heavy food, not suitable for me." Rather, the better course is to use another expression and say, "I have a barrier preventing me from eating, and in my house I also do not eat anything." This is indicated by Allah's words: ﴿and they gave him good news of a boy,﴾ in that they made him understand that they are not among those who eat, and they did not say, "Food and drink are not suitable for us."

Then another etiquette in giving good news: a person should not be told what pleases him all at once, for that may produce an illness. This is indicated by the fact that they sat, and Ibrahim, peace be upon him, became at ease with them. Then they said, ﴿We give you good news,﴾ then they mentioned the nobler of the two kinds, which is the male, and they were not satisfied with that until they described him with the best descriptions. For the son is less than the daughter when the daughter is perfect in form and good in character, and the son is the opposite. Then they left aside all the other attributes, such as beauty, good looks, strength and soundness, and chose knowledge, to indicate that knowledge is the head of the attributes and the chief of the qualities. We have already mentioned the benefit of putting the good news before the announcement of the destruction of the people of Lut, so that he would know that Allah destroys them and replaces them with a successor, bringing in their place something better than them.

* * *

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then his wife came forward in a loud cry, and she struck her face and said, "An old barren woman!"﴾

That is, she came forward to her people, because she was in their service. When they spoke with her husband about her giving birth, she felt shy and turned away from them. So Allah mentioned that with the expression "came forward to the people," and did not say "turned away from the angels." Allah's words ﴿in a loud cry﴾ mean a shout, as is the custom of women when they hear something about their own circumstances: they cry out a customary cry at times of shyness or astonishment. It is possible to say that this cry was her saying, "Woe to me!" as indicated by the verse in Surat Hud. Striking the face is also one of their customs. She regarded this as unlikely because of two attributes combined:

The first: advanced age.

The second: barrenness, because she had not borne children in her youth and the vigor of her prime. Then she became incapable and despaired, so she considered it unlikely. It is as if she said, "Would that you had made a prayer close to being answered," thinking that this came from them, as a guest may utter prayers in the form of statements, like the words of one who prays: "May Allah give you wealth and grant you a child." But they said: this from us is not a prayer. Rather, it is the word of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "So says your Lord."﴾ Then they dismissed her doubt with their words: ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing.﴾

We have mentioned the explanation of these two names many times. If it is asked, why did He say here ﴿the All-Wise, the All-Knowing﴾ and in Hud ﴿Praiseworthy, Glorious﴾ [Hud: 73], we say: because what we have explained is that the narration there is more detailed. They mentioned there what removes the sense of unlikelihood with their words: ﴿Do you wonder at the command of Allah?﴾ [Hud: 73]. Then, when she accepted it, they guided her to thank the blessings of Allah and reminded her of His favor with their words "(Praiseworthy)", because the Praiseworthy is the One from whom good acts are truly realized. Their words ﴿Glorious﴾ indicate that one of supreme and lofty aspiration does not praise Him merely for His beautiful act, but praises Him and glorifies Him for His own essence. Here, since they did not say ﴿Do you wonder?﴾, they pointed to what removes her astonishment by alerting her to His wisdom and His knowledge. There is a subtle point in this: that this order is observed in both surahs. The Praiseworthy relates to the act, and the Glorious relates to the word. Likewise, the All-Wise is the One whose act is fitting for His knowledge, done intentionally for that purpose, unlike one whose act happens to coincide with the desired end by chance, such as someone who turns over in his sleep and kills a snake while asleep. Such a person is not called wise. But if he performs an act intending to kill the snake in a way that keeps him safe from its bite, he is called wise in that act. The All-Knowing refers to the essence, indicating that He deserves praise for His glory, even if He does not perform an act while intending it by His knowledge, and even if He does not act in accordance with what He intends.

* * *

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿He said, "What is your business, O messengers?"﴾ In this there are issues:

If it is asked, what required that his words be introduced with "fa" (then), and had it been as you say, he would have said, "What is this hurry, and what is your urgent business?" We say: had he felt fear of them and they left without giving good news or bringing comfort, he would not have said anything. But when they brought him comfort, he said: ﴿What is your business,﴾ meaning, after this great comfort, what is this painful alarm?

Second issue: Is there a benefit in the word khatb (matter, business) that is not found in other words? We say: Yes, because the single words that come close to it are shaghl (occupation), amr (affair) and fi'l (act) and the like, and none of these indicates the greatness of a matter. But khatb is a great matter, and the greatness of a matter indicates the greatness of the one by whose hand it is accomplished. So he said: ﴿What is your khatb?﴾, meaning, because of your greatness, you are sent only on a great matter. Had he said it in a compound phrase, such as "What is your weighty occupation and your great affair?", it would have been lengthy. So khatb conveyed magnification together with brevity.

**Third issue: How was it known that they were messengers?** We say: they said it to him, as the proof of the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, we have been sent to the people of Lot﴾ [Hud: 70]. It was not mentioned here because we have explained that the full narrative is recorded in Surat Hud. Alternatively, we say: when they said to his wife, ﴿Thus has your Lord said﴾, he knew that they had been sent down from Allah, since they were relaying the word of Allah the Exalted. This is supported by the fact that their statement, ﴿Indeed, we have been sent to a people of criminals﴾, was the answer to his question to them.

**Fourth issue:** This is the very same narrative that is related in Hud. There they said, ﴿Indeed, we have been sent﴾ after the fear had left him and they had given him good news. Here they said, ﴿Indeed, we have been sent﴾ after he asked them about the matter. Also, there they said, ﴿Indeed, we have been sent to the people of Lot﴾ [Hud: 70], and here they said, ﴿Indeed, we have been sent to a people of criminals﴾. The narration is from their words. If they did not say that, the question would still arise. We say: if someone, relating from Zayd, says, "Zayd said, 'Amr went out,'" and then says again, "Zayd said, 'Indeed Bakr went out,'" then either Zayd uttered two statements, or the speaker is not relating what Zayd said.

The answer to the first is that when he (Abraham) became afraid, it is possible that they had not said to him, ﴿Do not fear, indeed we have been sent to the people of Lot﴾ [Hud: 70]. Then, when he said to them, "What is your business?" they could say, ﴿Indeed, we have been sent to the people of Lot﴾, in order to destroy them, just as a speaker says, "I went out of the house," and it is asked, "Why did you go out?" and he says, "I went out to trade." But here there is a meaningful benefit: they only said, in answer to ﴿What is your business?﴾, that they would destroy them by the command of Allah, so that their innocence of harming the innocent and neglecting the wrongdoer would be known. So they repeated the word "sending."

As for the second: we say that the narration may be a narration of the wording, as when you say, "Zayd said, 'I passed by Amr,'" and he relates his exact words. And it may be a narration of his speech in its meaning. You say, "Zayd said that Amr went out," and you may, on another occasion, in a different narration, change the wording to another word. You say, "When Zayd said that Bakr went out, I said such and such." Similarly here: the Qur'an is an inimitable (mu'jiz) wording, and what came from those before our Prophet (peace be upon him), whether from them or revealed to them, its wording was not inimitable. So it follows that these narrations are not in those exact words. Thus it is as if they said to him, ﴿Indeed, we have been sent to a people of criminals﴾, and they said, ﴿Indeed, we have been sent to the people of Lot﴾ [Hud: 70]. He may say, "Indeed, we have been sent to the people of one who believes in you," because he does not relate their wording in a way that requires it to be identical; rather he relates their speech in its meaning, and he has many expressions. Do you not see that when the Exalted related their wording of the greeting in one of the interpretations, He said in both places, ﴿Salaman﴾ and ﴿Salam﴾? Then He explained the purpose for which they were sent with His words: ﴿to send down upon them stones of clay﴾. We have explained this in Surat al-'Ankabut, and we said that this is evidence for the obligation of stoning the one who commits sodomy.

There are several issues in this:

**First issue:** What need is there for a group of angels when one of them could overturn the cities with a feather from his wing? We say: a powerful king may order a lowly person to destroy an important man, and he may order an important man to serve a lowly person, to demonstrate the effectiveness of his command. Since He destroyed a great multitude with lice, locusts and gnats, indeed with the wind by which there is life, this was more manifest in power. And since He ordered thousands of angels to destroy the people of Badr despite their small number, this was more manifest in the effectiveness of the command. There is another benefit: whoever is under the obedience of a great king, and an enemy appears to him, and he seeks the help of the king, and the king helps him with his most senior soldiers, this is an honouring of him by the king. The more numerous the enemy and the more abundant the reinforcement, the more complete the honour. But Allah the Exalted helped Lot with ten (angels), and our Prophet (peace be upon him) with five thousand. The difference between the two numbers is clear. We have mentioned some of this in the explanation of His words, ﴿And We did not send down upon his people after him any army from the heaven﴾ [Ya-Sin: 28].

**Second issue:** What is the benefit of emphasising the stones by describing them as ﴿of clay﴾? We say: because some people call hail "stones," so His words, ﴿of clay﴾, remove that misunderstanding. Know that some of those who claim to reason say: nothing descends from the sky except stones of clay, rounded like hailstones and like the pellets that archers make. They said: the cause of this is that a whirlwind raises dust from the great wastelands where there is no habitation, and the winds carry it to some lands. It happens that it reaches moist air, and it becomes wet clay. When wet clay descends and disperses, it becomes round, as is proven by the fact that if you throw water upward and then look at it, you will see it fall in round drops like large pearls. Then, while it is falling, if it happens that the fires that are in the atmosphere strike it, they turn it into stones like baked brick, and it descends and strikes whomever Allah has decreed to destroy. It often descends in places where there is no habitation, so it is not seen and not known about. For this reason He said, ﴿of clay﴾, because what is not ﴿of clay﴾, like the stone in thunderbolts, does not occur in such quantity that it rains down. But this is far-fetched. A person of complete intellect would base his thinking on what that speaker said, and would say: that whirlwind, when it occurred, if it occurred due to another event, this leads to an infinite regress, and there must be a termination at a Creator who is not created. That Creator must be an agent who chooses. The one who chooses may do what was mentioned, and may create stones of clay in another way, without fire or dust. However, the intellect has no path to certainty about the manner of its creation, and what the intellect cannot reach must be taken from transmitted reports. The text has come with it, so we accept it, and we do not know the manner. What is known is that the descent of stones of clay from the sky is more strange and more wondrous than other things, because normally they must remain in the fire.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 51, verse 34–36:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Marked by your Lord for the transgressors﴾. Regarding this there are several opinions.

The first: each one of them has written upon it the name of the person who will be killed by it.

The second: they were created with their names and for their punishment, unlike the rest of the stones, which were created for use in buildings and other things.

The third: they were sent against the criminals, because the word irsal (sending) is used for grazing animals; one says "arsalaha li-tar'a" (he sent it to graze), so it is permissible to say sawwamaha (he marked it) in the sense of arsalaha (he sent it). It is in this sense that His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and the marked horses﴾ (Surah Al 'Imran: 14) is interpreted, indicating independence from them and that they are not for riding, so that this is more indicative of wealth, as He said: ﴿and the heaped-up hoards of gold and silver﴾ (Surah Al 'Imran: 14). His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿for the transgressors﴾ indicates the opposite of what the naturalists (al-tabi'iyyun) say: that when a stone strikes one of the people, that is a kind of coincidence (ittifaq), for it falls by its nature and it happens to a person and strikes him. So His saying ﴿marked﴾ means: at the very beginning when it was created and sent. Once this is known, that was only with the intention of destroying the transgressors. If it is said: if the stones are marked for the transgressors, how did they say ﴿Indeed we have been sent to a people who are criminals﴾ and ﴿to send upon them﴾, although the transgressor (musrif) is other than the criminal (mujrim) in language? We say: the criminal is the one who commits a great sin, for in the root jurm there is an indication of greatness, and from it comes jurm of a thing for the greatness of its size. The transgressor is the one who commits a major sin, and whoever transgresses, even in minor sins, becomes a criminal, because a small thing added to a small thing becomes great. Whoever commits a crime has also transgressed, because he has committed a major sin even if all at once; so the two attributes are combined in them. However, there is in this a subtle spiritual point: God, Exalted is He, marked them for the persistent transgressor who does not give up the crime. Knowledge of future matters belongs to God, Exalted is He; He knows that they are transgressors, so He commanded the angels to send them upon them. As for the angels, their knowledge relates to the present, and they were criminals, so they said: ﴿Indeed we have been sent to a people﴾, we know them to be criminals, ﴿so that we may send upon them stones﴾ created for whoever does not believe, persists, and transgresses. It follows from this that our knowledge is that if they had lived for years, they would have persisted in crime. If it is said: is the lam for generic definition (ta'rif al-jins) or for definition of reference (ta'rif al-'ahd)? We say: for definition of reference, i.e. marked for these transgressors, since not every transgressor has a marked stone. If it is said: what was their transgression? We say: what is indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿No one in the worlds has preceded you in it﴾ (Surah Al A'raf: 80), i.e. no one reached your level.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So We brought out whoever was in it of the believers﴾ has two benefits:

The first: demonstrating power and choice, for whoever says it is by chance says it strikes the righteous and the wicked alike; when God distinguished the criminal from the good-doer, this indicates choice.

The second: demonstrating that by the blessing of the good-doer the offender is saved, for the town was not destroyed as long as a believer was in it. The pronoun refers to the town, which is understood even though it was not mentioned.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Yet We found in it no house except a house of those who submit﴾ contains an indication that when disbelief prevails and wickedness spreads, the worship of believers does not benefit alongside it. This is unlike the case where most of creation follows the straight path, while among them there is a small group who steal and commit fornication. Some have offered an analogy for this: the world is like a body, the presence of the righteous is like wholesome foods, hot and cold, and the disbelievers and the wicked are like the poisons that enter it and harm it. Then, if the body is empty of benefits while harms are in it, it perishes; if it is free of harms while benefits are in it, its life is good and it grows. If both are found in it, the judgment follows the dominant element. So it is with lands and their people.

The evidence that "muslim" means "believer" is clear. But the truth is that "muslim" is more general than "believer," and applying a general term to a specific one is not impermissible. Thus, when a believer is called "muslim," this does not indicate that the two concepts are identical. It is as if He, Exalted is He, had said: "We brought out the believers. We found none of the more general category among them except one house of those who submit." This implies that there were no others there who were believers. This is like when someone asks another, "Who is in the house among people?" and he replies, "No animal in the house is there except Zayd." He is informing him that the house is empty of every human being other than Zayd.

* * *

Then He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And We left in it a sign for those who fear the painful punishment﴾.

There is disagreement concerning this sign. It has been said: it is a foul, black water, because their land split and that water came out of it. It has also been said: it is stones cast upon their dwellings, and these lie between Syria and the Hijaz. His saying, ﴿for those who fear the painful punishment﴾, means that the one who benefits from it is the one who fears. As He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿for a people who reason﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 35] in Surat al-'Ankabut. There is a difference between the two in wording. Here He said "a sign" (ayah), and there He said "a clear sign" (ayah bayyinah) [al-'Ankabut: 35]. There He said "for a people who reason," and here He said "for those who fear." Is there a difference in meaning? We say: there, what is mentioned is in the most eloquent manner indicated by His saying, "a clear sign," in that He described it with manifestness. Likewise, "from it" (minha) and "in it" (fiha): the particle "min" indicates partiality. So it is as if He had said: "From its very self there is for you a lasting sign." Likewise He said, "for a people who reason," since the one who reasons is more general than the one who fears, so the sign there was more evident. The reason for this is what we have mentioned: the aim there was to frighten the people, while here the aim is to console the heart. Do you not see His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So We brought out whoever was in it of the believers﴾ ﴿Yet We found in it no house except a house of those who submit﴾? And He said there: ﴿We will surely save you and your family﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 33], without a full explanation of the salvation of the Muslims and the believers altogether.

And in Musa (Moses) as well, when We sent him to Fir'awn (Pharaoh) with a clear authority. But he turned away with his force, and said, "A sorcerer or a madman."

His saying, ﴿And in Musa﴾, may be understood as conjoined to something already known, or as conjoined to something already mentioned. As for the first, there are several opinions.

The first: that what is meant is the same as in Ibrahim, and in Musa, because whoever mentions Ibrahim knows this.

The second: for your people there is a lesson in Lut and his people, and in Musa and Fir'awn.

The third: that there is the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: "Reflect upon Ibrahim and Lut and their people, and upon Musa and Fir'awn," and all of these are close to one another.

As for the second, there are also several opinions.

The first of them: that it is conjoined to His saying: ﴿And in the earth are signs for those who are certain﴾, so ﴿And in Musa﴾ — and this is distant, because of its distance in mention and because there is no connection between them.

The second: that it is conjoined to His saying: ﴿And We left in it a sign for those who fear﴾, so ﴿And in Musa﴾ means: "And We placed in Musa," in the manner of their saying: "I fed her straw and cold water," and "I girded myself with a sword and a spear." This is closer, but it is not free of strain if we say, as some exegetes have said, that the pronoun in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And We left in it﴾, refers to the town.

The third: we say that "in it" refers to the narrative, so the sense is: "And We left in their narrative a sign," or "in their story," so that it becomes: "And in the story of Musa is a sign." This is close to the first possibility, which is conjoining to the known.

The fourth: that it is conjoined to "Has there come to you the report of the guests of Ibrahim?" and its implied sense is: "And in Musa there is a report when We sent him." This is fitting, since Allah has gathered much mention of Ibrahim and Musa, peace be upon them both, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Or has he not been informed of what is in the scriptures of Musa﴾ ﴿and of Ibrahim who fulfilled [his trust]﴾ [al-Najm: 36–37], and He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The scriptures of Ibrahim and Musa﴾. And "sultan" means strength through proof and evidence, and "mubin" means that which distinguishes. We have mentioned that what is meant by it may be the decisive proofs that he had, with which he argued against Fir'awn; and it may be that what is meant is the miracle that distinguishes between the magic of the sorcerer and the affair of the messengers.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But he turned away with his force﴾, there are several opinions:

The first: the "ba'" (with) denotes accompaniment, and "al-rukn" is an indication of the people, as if He, exalted is He, were saying: "He turned away together with his people." It is said: "So-and-so camped with his army at such-and-such place." And this opinion is supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So he showed him the greatest sign﴾ ﴿but he denied and disobeyed﴾ ﴿then he turned his back, striving﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 22–23]. He said "turned his back" (adbara), which has the meaning of "turned away" (tawalla). And His saying: ﴿Then he gathered [his people] and called out﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 23] has the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿with his force﴾.

The second: ﴿Fa-tawalla﴾ means he took a helper, and the "ba'" is then for transitivity, meaning he strengthened himself with his soldiers.

The third: he took charge of Musa's affair by his own strength, as if he said: "I will kill Musa lest he change your religion and lest he cause corruption in the earth." So he took charge of his affair himself, and in this case the object is not mentioned. His "rukn" is his own strong self. It is possible that what is meant by his "rukn" is Haman, for he was his minister, and on this second opinion this is more apparent.

﴿And he said, "A sorcerer or a madman."﴾ That is: "This is a sorcerer or a madman." As for His saying, ﴿a sorcerer﴾, it means he brings the jinn with his magic or draws near to them, and the jinn draw near to him and intend him, even if he does not intend them. So the sorcerer and the madman both have their affair with the jinn, except that the sorcerer comes to them by his own choice, while the madman is come to by them without his choice. So it is as if he (Fir'awn) intended to safeguard his speech from falsehood, and so he said: he either enchants the jinn or is enchanted; if he has no knowledge of it and does not intend it, then the jinn come to him.

And in Musa (Moses) as well, when We sent him to Fir'awn (Pharaoh) with a clear authority. But he turned away with his force, and said, "A sorcerer or a madman."

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 51, verses 42–43:**

Allah's words: ﴿It leaves nothing it comes upon without making it like crumbled dust.﴾ On this verse there are several discussions.

**The first: on its i'rab (grammatical analysis).** There are two possibilities.

The first is that it is in the accusative as a description (ṣifah) of the wind, following the description "barren" (al-ʿaqīm). Al-Wahidi mentioned that it is a description. But if it is asked, "How can it be a description when a definite noun cannot be described by clauses, and ﴿مَا تَذَرُ﴾ is a clause, and only indefinite nouns are described by it?" we answer that the reply to this has two aspects.

The first: it is a description by implicit repetition of the wind, as if he said: "And We sent upon them the barren wind, a wind that leaves nothing."

The second: the definite noun is indefinite in meaning, because that wind is unspecified, as if he said: "And We sent the wind which was not one of the winds that occur, and the like of it has not occurred. Because of its severity it is unspecified." For this reason, when he mentioned it in the Qur'an, he mentioned it in the indefinite and described it with a clause from among its clauses, such as the words of the Exalted: ﴿Rather, it is that which you sought to hasten: a wind in which is a painful punishment﴾ (al-Ahqaf: 24), and so on.

The second possibility, which is the more correct, is that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). You say: "There came to me one who understands something, so I taught him and made him understand," meaning: his state was such. If it is asked, "The state of the sending was not ﴿مَا تَذَرُ﴾, and the state should exist together with its bearer at the time of the action, so it is not permissible to say, 'Zayd came to me yesterday riding tomorrow,' and the wind, after it was sent for a time, became one that leaves nothing as a thing," we answer: what is meant is the explanation by potentiality, that is, We sent it while it had the strength and capacity to leave nothing. We say to one who came and stayed with you for days and then asked you something: "You came to me asking," meaning, before the asking, by potentiality and possibility. This is if we say it is in the accusative, which is the well-known view. It is also possible that it is in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimated form being: "It is one that leaves nothing."

**The second discussion:** ﴿مَا تَذَرُ﴾ is a negation of the present moment of speech. One says: "ما يخرج زيد" meaning "Zayd is not going out now." When you want the future, you say: "لا يخرج" or "لن يخرج." As for the past, you say: "ما خرج" and "لم يخرج." The wind, at the time of speaking with the Prophet (ﷺ), was one that left nothing without making it like crumbled dust. So how does he say with the expression of the present state: ﴿مَا تَذَرُ﴾? We answer: the narration is taken as estimated, on the basis that it is narrated as it was at the time of the event. For this reason the Exalted said: ﴿And their dog stretched out its two forelegs at the threshold﴾ (al-Kahf: 18), although the active participle of the past does not govern, and only that which has the meaning of the present and the future governs.

**The third discussion:** Is there in the words of the Exalted ﴿مَا تَذَرُ مِن شَيْءٍ أَتَتْ عَلَيْهِ﴾ an intensification and the entry of a restriction, as in His words: ﴿destroying everything by the command of its Lord﴾ (al-Ahqaf: 25)? We answer: it is as it has occurred, because His words ﴿أَتَتْ عَلَيْهِ﴾ are a description of ﴿شَيْءٍ﴾, as if He said: "Everything it came upon, or everything it comes upon, it made like crumbled dust." The heavens do not enter into this, because it did not come upon them. What enters into it is the bodies over which the winds blow. If it is asked: "But the mountains and the rocks were come upon by it, and it did not make them like crumbled dust?" we answer: what is meant is that it came upon them deliberately, and these were ʿĀd and their buildings and their roofs. This is because it was commanded by an order from Allah, so it was as if it was intending them. Thus it did not leave any of those things without making it like crumbled dust. Moreover, the ṣirr is the cold wind, and the repeated form does not separate from the meaning that is in the word without repetition. You say: "ḥaththa" and "ḥathḥatha," and in ḥathḥatha is what is in ḥaththa.

Page 192

On this there are two views:

The first: it was cold, and it was during the days of the "ʿAjuz," which are eight days from the end of Shubat and the beginning of Adhar. The cold wind, because of the severity of its cold, burns trees and fruits and other things and blackens them.

The second: it was hot, and the ṣirr is the intense one, not the cold one. The words of the Exalted ﴿in a ṣarrah﴾ are explained by intensity, that is, in an intensity of heat.

**The fourth discussion:** In the words of the Exalted ﴿مَا تَذَرُ مِن شَيْءٍ أَتَتْ عَلَيْهِ إِلَّا جَعَلَتْهُ كَالرَّمِيمِ﴾, because in His words ﴿مَا تَذَرُ﴾ there is the negation of leaving together with the affirmation of coming upon, it is as if the Exalted said: "It comes upon things and does not leave them unburnt." The saying of one who says, "It came upon a thing and made it thus," implies the negation of coming upon what it did not make thus.

As for His words ﴿وَفِي ثَمُودَ﴾, the discussion of it and of ʿĀd is what preceded in His words ﴿وَفِي مُوسَىٰ﴾.

As for His words ﴿إِذْ قِيلَ لَهُمْ تَمَتَّعُوا حَتَّىٰ حِينٍ﴾, some of the exegetes said: what is meant by it is that Allah gave them respite for three days after they slaughtered the she-camel, and during those days their colours changed, so their faces turned yellow and blackened. But this is weak, because the words of the Exalted ﴿فَعَتَوْا عَنْ أَمْرِ رَبِّهِمْ﴾ (al-Dhariyat: 44), with the particle of the fāʾ (then), are evidence that the insolence was after His words ﴿تَمَتَّعُوا﴾. Therefore the apparent meaning is that what is meant is what Allah has determined for people of the terms of life. There is no one except that he is given respite for the duration of his term, and it is said to him: "Enjoy yourself until the end of your term. If you do well, you have obtained enjoyment in both abodes; otherwise, you have no share in the Hereafter."

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿But they acted arrogantly against the command of their Lord, so the thunderbolt seized them while they were looking on.﴾ Here there is a point of inquiry. ʿatā (to act arrogantly) is used with ʿan, and it is also used with ʿalā. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then We will surely drag out from every group those who were most insolent toward the Most Merciful.﴾ [Maryam: 69]. Here it is used with ʿan. We say: it carries the meaning of istiʿtāʾ (being overbearing). So where He says ﴿against the command of their Lord﴾, it is like His saying ﴿They do not disdain to worship Him﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 206]. Where He says ʿalā, it is like the speaker's saying: "So-and-so acts haughtily against us." The thunderbolt (al-ṣāʿiqah) has two meanings here, which we have mentioned.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the people of Noah before them; indeed they were a defiant people﴾. It has been read as "qawma" in the genitive and in the accusative. What is the grammatical basis of each?

You say: "In so-and-so there is a lesson, and in so-and-so and so-and-so." As for the accusative, it is by estimating: "And We destroyed the people of Noah before"; because what preceded indicates destruction, so it is coordinated with the position (ʿaṭf ʿalā al-maḥall). On this reading His saying ﴿before (min qablu)﴾ has an obvious meaning, as if He were saying: "And We destroyed the people of Noah before." As for the first reading, its estimate is: "And in the people of Noah there is a lesson for you from before Thamud and ʿĀd and others."

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the heaven, We built it with power, and indeed We are expanding it﴾. This is a demonstration of divine oneness (tawḥīd), whereas what preceded was a demonstration of the gathering (ḥashr).

As for His saying here: ﴿And the heaven, We built it with power﴾, while you know that what you worship besides God did not create any part of it, so association (ishrāk) is not valid. It may be said that this is a return, after the threat, to establishing the proof. The building of the heaven is evidence of the power to create bodies again, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the like of them?﴾ [Yasin: 81]. Concerning this there are several issues.

The first issue: the accusative by way of explanation (naṣb ʿalā sharīṭat al-tafsīr) is preferred in some places. If the coordination is with a verbal clause, what is that clause? We say: in some of the aspects we mentioned in His saying ﴿And ʿĀd and Thamud﴾ [al-Tawbah: 70], its estimate is: "And has the story of ʿĀd come to you? And has the story of Thamud come to you?" coordinated with His saying: ﴿Has there come to you the story of Abraham's honored guests?﴾. On this, what preceded is a verbal clause, with no obscurity. On the other reading, the prepositional phrase in the accusative is closer to the accusative than to the nominative, so coordinating it with what is in the accusative is preferable. Moreover, His saying ﴿so We cast them off (fa-nabadhnāhum)﴾, His saying ﴿We sent (arsalnā)﴾, His saying ﴿so the thunderbolt seized them (fa-akhadhathumu al-ṣāʿiqah)﴾, and ﴿so they were not able (fa-mā istaṭāʿū)﴾ are all verbal clauses, so the accusative became preferred.

The second issue: He repeated the mention of building in connection with the heavens. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the sky and He who built it﴾ [al-Shams: 5]; He said: ﴿Is the sky, He built it?﴾ [al-Naziʿat: 27]; and He said: ﴿He made for you the earth as a resting place and the sky as a structure﴾ [Ghafir: 64]. What is the wisdom in this? We say there are several aspects.

The first: the building remains until the Resurrection; nothing has fallen from it and no part of it has perished. As for the earth, it is in change and alteration; it is like a carpet that is spread out, folded up, and moved. The heaven is like a firm, established structure, and to this refers His saying: ﴿seven firm ones﴾ [al-Naba: 12]. As for the lands, how many of them have become seas and then returned to land since their creation?

The second: the heaven is seen like a dome built above the heads, while the earth is spread out and expanded. Building is more fitting for what is raised, as He said: ﴿He raised its height﴾ [al-Naziʿat: 28].

The third: some of the sages said: the heaven is the dwelling place of spirits, and the earth is the place of deeds, and dwelling is more fitting to being a structure. And God knows best.

The third issue: the principle is that the agent precedes the object of the action, and the verb is the agent. His saying "We built (banaynā)" is the agent for "the heaven." What is the wisdom in placing the object before the verb? If He had said "And We built the heaven with power," it would have been more concise. We say: in the view of the one who looks for knowledge, the Maker comes before the making. Since the intended aim was to establish knowledge of the Maker, the evidence was put first, so He said: "And the heaven, the adorned one about which you have no doubt, We built it. Recognize Us through it, if you do not know Us."

The fourth issue: if the intended aim is to establish divine oneness, why did He say ﴿We built it (banaynāhā)﴾ rather than "I built it" or "God built it"? We say: His saying "We built (banaynā)" is more indicative of the absence of a partner in the action and of sole authority, whereas "I built it (banaytuhā)" could allow for association. The complete argument is that His saying ﴿We built it﴾ does not create the illusion that the gods they worshipped are those to which the pronoun in ﴿We built it﴾ refers. For those are either carved idols, or stars which they made idols in the forms and natures of. As for the carved idols, they do not doubt that they built nothing of the heaven. As for the stars, they are in the heaven and need it, so they cannot be its builder. It can only be said that they were built for it and their places were made for them. Since what they claimed was not imagined, He said: "We built it, We, and We are other than what they say and call upon; so they are not fit to be partners with Us, because whatever is other than the heaven and below it in rank cannot be the creator and builder of the heaven."

Therefore it is known that the intended meaning is the plural of majesty (jamʿ al-taʿẓīm), and the text conveys His greatness. Majesty is most negating of a partner, so it is established that His saying ﴿We built it (banaynāhā)﴾ indicates the negation of a partner more than "I built it" or "God built it."

If it is said: why do you say that the plural indicates majesty? We say: the answer is from two aspects.

The first: speech is according to the understanding of the listener, and the listener is a human being, and a human being measures the unseen by the seen. For the great person among them is one who does a thing through his soldiers and servants and does not personally undertake it, so the king says "We did," meaning his servants did it by our command, and there is majesty in that. Likewise with regard to the Unseen.

The second aspect: when a statement comes from one person and the others are content with it, the speaker says "we all did such-and-such." If you understand this, then God, exalted is He, whenever He commands the doing of something, no one can reject it, and each one is submissive to it, and he says "we did" instead of "I did." For this Great King, "we all" applies such that no one denies it and no soul resists it. His saying ﴿with power (bi-aydin)﴾ means with strength, and aid (al-ayd) means strength. This is the well-known view, and it is how His saying ﴿Possessor of power (dhā al-ayd); indeed he was one who returned repeatedly﴾ [Sad: 17] is explained. It may be said that the intended meaning is the plural of hand (yad), and the proof is that He said: ﴿What I created with My two hands (bi-yadayya)﴾ [Sad: 75], and He said: ﴿Of what Our hands have made, livestock﴾ [Yasin: 71]. If it had come upon them in heedlessness, a suspicious person might imagine that they were seized unawares, like one seized suddenly and unprepared, just as a brave challenger says: "I informed you of my intention to confront you, so await me."

His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿So they were not able to stand up﴾ may bear two meanings.

The first: it is to demonstrate their inability to flee or escape, by way of hyperbole, for one who cannot stand up, how can he walk, let alone flee? On this reading there are verbal subtleties.

The first of them: His saying ﴿so they were not able (fa-mā istaṭāʿū)﴾. The word istiṭāʿah is weaker than qudrah (power), because istiṭāʿah contains an indication of seeking, and that signifies lack of power and independence. Whoever is able (istaṭāʿa) to do something is below one who has power over it. For this reason the theologians (al-mutakallimūn) say: istiṭāʿah accompanying the act or preceding it is an indication of a required power from God, exalted is He, taken from Him. And His saying ﴿so they were not able (fa-mā istaṭāʿū)﴾ is more emphatic than the speaker's saying "they had no power to stand up."

The second: His saying ﴿of standing (min qiyām)﴾ with the addition of min, and you have known its emphasis.

The third: His saying ﴿standing (qiyām)﴾ replaces His saying "fleeing (harab)," because we have shown that one who cannot stand is more incapable of fleeing.

The second meaning: that the intended sense of ﴿of standing﴾ is standing up for the matter, that is, they were not able to stand up for it.

One who cannot do that fights and defends himself with everything he can, because he defends his soul, yet they were nonetheless not victorious. You know that the saying "he is not one who is victorious (mā huwa bi-muntaṣir)" is more emphatic than "he did not and does not triumph." His saying ﴿triumphed (intaṣara)﴾ [al-Shura: 41] means: for something within his nature that this is so, just as you say "So-and-so does not help," or "So-and-so does not help."

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the people of Noah before them; indeed they were a defiant people﴾. It has been read as "qawma" in the genitive and in the accusative. What is the grammatical basis of each?

We say: as for the genitive, it is clear, being coordinated (ʿaṭf) with what came before in His saying: ﴿And in ʿĀd, and in Moses﴾. You say: "In so-and-so there is a lesson, and in so-and-so and so-and-so." As for the accusative, it is by estimating: "And We destroyed the people of Noah before"; because what preceded indicates destruction, so it is coordinated with the position (ʿaṭf ʿalā al-maḥall). On this reading His saying ﴿before (min qablu)﴾ has an obvious meaning, as if He were saying: "And We destroyed the people of Noah before." As for the first reading, its estimate is: "And in the people of Noah there is a lesson for you from before Thamud and ʿĀd and others."

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the heaven, We built it with power, and indeed We are expanding it﴾. This is a demonstration of divine oneness (tawḥīd), whereas what preceded was a demonstration of the gathering (ḥashr).

As for His saying here: ﴿And the heaven, We built it with power﴾, while you know that what you worship besides God did not create any part of it, so association (ishrāk) is not valid. It may be said that this is a return, after the threat, to establishing the proof. The building of the heaven is evidence of the power to create bodies again, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the like of them?﴾ [Yasin: 81]. Concerning this there are several issues.

The first issue: the accusative by way of explanation (naṣb ʿalā sharīṭat al-tafsīr) is preferred in some places. If the coordination is with a verbal clause, what is that clause? We say: in some of the aspects we mentioned in His saying ﴿And ʿĀd and Thamud﴾ [al-Tawbah: 70], its estimate is: "And has the story of ʿĀd come to you? And has the story of Thamud come to you?" coordinated with His saying: ﴿Has there come to you the story of Abraham's honored guests?﴾. On this, what preceded is a verbal clause, with no obscurity. On the other reading, the prepositional phrase in the accusative is closer to the accusative than to the nominative, so coordinating it with what is in the accusative is preferable. Moreover, His saying ﴿so We cast them off (fa-nabadhnāhum)﴾, His saying ﴿We sent (arsalnā)﴾, His saying ﴿so the thunderbolt seized them (fa-akhadhathumu al-ṣāʿiqah)﴾, and ﴿so they were not able (fa-mā istaṭāʿū)﴾ are all verbal clauses, so the accusative became preferred.

The second issue: He repeated the mention of building in connection with the heavens. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the sky and He who built it﴾ [al-Shams: 5]; He said: ﴿Is the sky, He built it?﴾ [al-Naziʿat: 27]; and He said: ﴿He made for you the earth as a resting place and the sky as a structure﴾ [Ghafir: 64]. What is the wisdom in this? We say there are several aspects.

The first: the building remains until the Resurrection; nothing has fallen from it and no part of it has perished. As for the earth, it is in change and alteration; it is like a carpet that is spread out, folded up, and moved. The heaven is like a firm, established structure, and to this refers His saying: ﴿seven firm ones﴾ [al-Naba: 12]. As for the lands, how many of them have become seas and then returned to land since their creation?

The second: the heaven is seen like a dome built above the heads, while the earth is spread out and expanded. Building is more fitting for what is raised, as He said: ﴿He raised its height﴾ [al-Naziʿat: 28].

The third: some of the sages said: the heaven is the dwelling place of spirits, and the earth is the place of deeds, and dwelling is more fitting to being a structure. And God knows best.

The third issue: the principle is that the agent precedes the object of the action, and the verb is the agent. His saying "We built (banaynā)" is the agent for "the heaven." What is the wisdom in placing the object before the verb? If He had said "And We built the heaven with power," it would have been more concise. We say: in the view of the one who looks for knowledge, the Maker comes before the making. Since the intended aim was to establish knowledge of the Maker, the evidence was put first, so He said: "And the heaven, the adorned one about which you have no doubt, We built it. Recognize Us through it, if you do not know Us."

The fourth issue: if the intended aim is to establish divine oneness, why did He say ﴿We built it (banaynāhā)﴾ rather than "I built it" or "God built it"? We say: His saying "We built (banaynā)" is more indicative of the absence of a partner in the action and of sole authority, whereas "I built it (banaytuhā)" could allow for association. The complete argument is that His saying ﴿We built it﴾ does not create the illusion that the gods they worshipped are those to which the pronoun in ﴿We built it﴾ refers. For those are either carved idols, or stars which they made idols in the forms and natures of. As for the carved idols, they do not doubt that they built nothing of the heaven. As for the stars, they are in the heaven and need it, so they cannot be its builder. It can only be said that they were built for it and their places were made for them. Since what they claimed was not imagined, He said: "We built it, We, and We are other than what they say and call upon; so they are not fit to be partners with Us, because whatever is other than the heaven and below it in rank cannot be the creator and builder of the heaven."

Therefore it is known that the intended meaning is the plural of majesty (jamʿ al-taʿẓīm), and the text conveys His greatness. Majesty is most negating of a partner, so it is established that His saying ﴿We built it (banaynāhā)﴾ indicates the negation of a partner more than "I built it" or "God built it."

If it is said: why do you say that the plural indicates majesty? We say: the answer is from two aspects.

The first: speech is according to the understanding of the listener, and the listener is a human being, and a human being measures the unseen by the seen. For the great person among them is one who does a thing through his soldiers and servants and does not personally undertake it, so the king says "We did," meaning his servants did it by our command, and there is majesty in that. Likewise with regard to the Unseen.

The second aspect: when a statement comes from one person and the others are content with it, the speaker says "we all did such-and-such." And when a group gathers on an act that cannot occur except through some of them, as when a large multitude and a great crowd go out to kill a beast and they kill it, it is said: "The people of such-and-such a town killed it," because all are content with it and all intended it. If you understand this, then God, exalted is He, whenever He commands the doing of something, no one can reject it, and each one is submissive to it, and he says "we did" instead of "I did." For this Great King, "we all" applies such that no one denies it and no soul resists it. His saying ﴿with power (bi-aydin)﴾ means with strength, and aid (al-ayd) means strength. This is the well-known view, and it is how His saying ﴿Possessor of power (dhā al-ayd); indeed he was one who returned repeatedly﴾ [Sad: 17] is explained. It may be said that the intended meaning is the plural of hand (yad), and the proof is that He said: ﴿What I created with My two hands (bi-yadayya)﴾ [Sad: 75], and He said: ﴿Of what Our hands have made, livestock﴾ [Yasin: 71]. If it is asked, why did He not say "We built it with Our hands" and instead say ﴿Of what Our hands have made﴾? We say: for a great benefit, namely that no one imagines the heaven to be created by other than God, whereas livestock is not like that. So there He said ﴿Of what Our hands have made﴾ [Sad: 71], explicitly stating that animals are created by God, exalted is He, without intermediary; and likewise ﴿I created with My two hands﴾ [Sad: 75]. And with the heaven, He said ﴿with power﴾ without the addition of a possessive, because it is not needed. There is another subtle point: there, having established the possessive after the pronoun referring to the object was omitted, He did not say "I created it with My two hands," nor "Our hands made it." Here He said ﴿We built it (banaynāhā)﴾, because there no one imagined that man was uncreated or that the animal was not made, so He did not say "I created him" or "I made it." As for the heaven, some ignorant people claim that it is not created, so He said ﴿We built it﴾ with the pronoun referring to it, to state explicitly that it is created.

His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And indeed We are expanding it (wa-innā lamūsiʿūn)﴾ has several meanings.

The first: it derives from expansion (siʿah), meaning We made it spacious, so that the earth and what surrounds it of water and air, in relation to the heaven and its vastness, is like a ring in a desert. The third: ﴿And indeed We are expanding it﴾ means providing sustenance to creation.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And of everything We created pairs﴾ (This is) an argument from what lies between them. The "pairs" (zawjān) are either opposites (ḍiddān), since male and female are like opposites, and the pair formed from them is likewise; or they are similar things (mutashākilān), since everything has a like, an equal, an opposite and a rival. The logicians (al-manṭiqiyyūn) said: what is meant by "thing" (shay') is the genus (jins), and the least that can be under a genus is two species (naw'ān). So from every genus He created two species: from substance (jawhar), for example, the material (māddī) and the immaterial (mujarrad); from the material, the growing (nāmī) and the inert (jāmid); from the growing, the perceiving (mudrik) and the plant (nabāt); and from the perceiving, the rational speaker (nāṭiq) and the silent (ṣāmit). All of this indicates that He is a single one (fard) with no multiplicity in Him.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿that perhaps you may remember﴾, it means: "that perhaps you may remember that the Creator of pairs cannot have a pair; for otherwise He would be contingent (mumkin), and thus created, and could not be a Creator." Or, ﴿that perhaps you may remember﴾ means: that the Creator of pairs is not incapable of gathering bodies (ḥashr al-ajsām) and assembling spirits (jam' al-arwāḥ).

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the earth — We spread it out, and how excellent are the spreaders!﴾ (This is) an argument from the earth, and the content of His saying ﴿And the earth — We spread it out﴾ is already known. In it there is evidence that the spreading (daḥw) of the earth came after the creation of the heaven, because the building of a house normally takes place before its carpeting. As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿how excellent are the spreaders!﴾, it means: "We are" — or, "how excellent are those who spread it out (māhidūhā)."

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And of everything We created pairs﴾ (This is) an argument from what lies between them. The "pairs" (zawjān) are either opposites (ḍiddān), since male and female are like opposites, and the pair formed from them is likewise; or they are similar things (mutashākilān), since everything has a like, an equal, an opposite and a rival. The logicians (al-manṭiqiyyūn) said: what is meant by "thing" (shay') is the genus (jins), and the least that can be under a genus is two species (naw'ān). So from every genus He created two species: from substance (jawhar), for example, the material (māddī) and the immaterial (mujarrad); from the material, the growing (nāmī) and the inert (jāmid); from the growing, the perceiving (mudrik) and the plant (nabāt); and from the perceiving, the rational speaker (nāṭiq) and the silent (ṣāmit). The first: His saying, ﴿flee﴾, indicates the speed of destruction, as if He were saying: destruction and punishment are swifter and closer than that the situation could tolerate any delay in returning. So hasten to God in alarm and flee.

The second: His saying, ﴿to God﴾, specifies the one fled toward. He did not mention that from which the flight is, for one of two reasons. Either because it is known, namely the terror of the punishment, or Satan, concerning whom He said: ﴿Indeed, Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy﴾ [Fatir: 6]. Or it is to be general, as if He were saying: everything other than God is your enemy, so flee to Him from everything besides Him. Its explanation is that everything besides Him destroys your capital, which is your life, and makes you miss what is truth and good. The destroyer of capital is an enemy that causes the loss of perfection. As for when you flee to God and turn to God, He takes your life but raises your affair and gives you a permanence with which there is no annihilation.

The third: the fa' (ف, "then") in ﴿fa-firru﴾ indicates sequence. Its meaning: when it is established that the Creator of the two pairs is one, then flee to Him and abandon everything else with a perpetual abandonment.
