Its explanation is that God, exalted, said: ﴿And the heaven We built with might﴾, ﴿and the earth We spread out﴾, and ﴿of everything We created pairs﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 47–49]. Then He made the speech directed to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: ﴿So flee to God; indeed, I am a clear warner to you from Him﴾, and He did not say "flee to Us." That is because variation in speech has an effect, and likewise variation in speakers has an effect. For this reason a person often gives advice to his son who has strayed from the right path, and varies the speech: sometimes encouragement, sometimes warning, and admonition through narrative. Then he says to another, "Speak with him, perhaps your words will benefit," because people's minds hold that variation of speakers and variation of speech are both influential. God, exalted, mentioned many kinds of speech, many proofs and signs, and a good portion of narratives, and then mentioned a speech from another speaker, namely the Prophet (ﷺ). Some exegetes say its implied sense is: "So say to them, 'Flee.'" His saying, ﴿Indeed, I am a warner to you from Him﴾, is an indication of the message (risalah).

There are also subtle points in it.

The first: God manifested His greatness by His saying, ﴿And the heaven We built﴾ and ﴿the earth We spread out﴾, and His awe by His saying, ﴿So We cast them into the sea﴾, and His saying, ﴿We sent upon them the barren wind﴾, and His saying, ﴿So the thunderbolt seized them﴾. In this is an indication that when He punishes, He is able to punish by means of that by which subsistence and existence are: earth, water, air and fire. The narratives of Lot indicate that the earth, from which existence and subsistence come, when God wills to make it a cause of annihilation; and likewise water, in the case of the people of Pharaoh; air, in the case of 'Ad; and fire, in the case of Thamud. Perhaps the ordering of the four narratives follows the order of the four elements, and we mentioned something of this in the commentary on Surat al-'Ankabut. Then, having shown His greatness and awe, He said to His Messenger: "Inform them of the situation and say: I am a messenger," by presenting the signs and recounting the narratives. So the mention of the Messenger after this has a benefit.

The second: in the message there are three things: the sender, the messenger, and the one to whom it is sent. Here He mentioned all of them. His saying, ﴿to you﴾, indicates the ones to whom it is sent; His saying, ﴿from Him﴾, indicates the sender; and His saying, ﴿a warner﴾, is an explanation of the messenger. He mentioned the one to whom it is sent first, because the one to whom it is sent is more intimately involved in the matter of the message, since the affair is completed through him. A king, if there were no one opposing or agreeing with him, would not send to him a warner or a bearer of good news, even if he were a great king. When there is an opponent or an agreer, he sends, even if the one addressed is not great. Then the sender is mentioned first because he is determined and is the one who initiates. As for the messenger, he is by choice. Were it not for the determined sender, the message would not be complete; but the messenger is not determined, because the King has the choice of whom He wills from among His servants. So He said, ﴿from Him﴾, then He said, ﴿a warner﴾, delaying the messenger after the sender.

The third: His saying, ﴿clear (mubin)﴾, is an indication of that by which the message is known, because every occurrence has a cause and a sign. The messenger is the one by whom the message is completed, and he must have a sign by which he is known. So His saying, ﴿clear﴾, is an indication of it, and it is either the proof (burhan) or the miracle (mu'jizah).

* * *

Then God, exalted, said: ﴿And do not set up with God another god﴾, completing the tawhid. This is because tawhid lies between ta'til (the negation of God) and tashrik (the association of partners), and the method of tawhid is the middle way. The one who negates says: there is no god at all; the polytheist says: in existence there are gods; and the monotheist says: the claim of two is false, and the negation of one is false. So His saying, ﴿So flee to God﴾, affirmed the existence of God, and when He said, ﴿And do not set up with God another god﴾, He negated more than one, so the tawhid is valid through the two verses. For this reason He said twice, ﴿Indeed, I am a clear warner to you from Him﴾, meaning in the two positions and the two places. We have mentioned many times that the one who negates, when he says there is no Necessary Existent, makes everything contingent, since every existent is contingent; yet God in reality is existent. Thus he has placed Him within the folds of his statement like the contingent things, and so he has associated (partners), making God like other than Him. And the polytheist, when he says that other than Him is a god, it follows from his statement that the god is not a god, according to what we mentioned in the explanation of the argument of mutual prevention (dalalat al-tamana'). Moreover, if there were gods in the heavens and the earth other than God, it would follow the incapacity of each one, so there would be no god in existence at all, and this would negate actual divinity, and so he would be a negator, and the negator is a polytheist, and the polytheist is a negator. Each of the two groups acknowledges that the other is in error, but each, on the other's doctrine, says that his own position is false, and he does not know it. Praise be to God who guided us. His saying, ﴿do not set up﴾, contains a subtle point: it is an indication that the gods are made (majul), not that God is taken. One might say: God is also "taken," by His saying, ﴿so take Him as trustee﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 9]. We answer: the answer to this is evident, and it has already been mentioned in His saying, exalted: ﴿And they took, besides God, gods﴾ [Ya-Sin: 74].

* * *

Then God, exalted, said: ﴿Thus, no messenger came to those before them except that they said, "A sorcerer or a madman."﴾

The exegesis is known from what has preceded, and we have mentioned that it indicates that the mention of narratives is for consolation. However, there is one subtle point here that we will not leave out: this verse is evidence that every messenger was denied, and then questions arise about it.

The first: among the prophets there were some who confirmed the religion of the prophet who came before them, and the people remained upon what they were upon, such as the prophets of the Children of Israel for a period. And how is it, since Adam, when he was sent, was not denied?

The second: what is the wisdom in God's decree that the messengers be denied, when He did not send a messenger with such multiplicity and variety of miracles that his contemporaries would believe him?

The third: His saying, ﴿no ... came ... except that they said﴾, is evidence that all of them said, "a sorcerer." But this is not so, because there was no messenger who did not have a people who believed in him, and they did not say that.

As for the answer to the first: we say that as for the one who confirmed (the previous religion), we do not concede that he is a messenger; rather he is a prophet upon the religion of a messenger, and whoever denies his messenger is necessarily also denying him.

As for the answer to the second: God sends a messenger only when people have need, and that occurs when unbelievers appear in the world, and unbelief does not appear except when ignorance is abundant. Moreover, God, exalted, does not send a messenger when belief in him is necessary, for otherwise belief in him would be the belief of despair and would not be accepted; and the ignorant person, if the one who makes clear to him is not in utmost clarity, does not accept him, and remains in the entanglement of misguidance. So this is a decree that has been necessitated by God's decree upon creation in this manner. We have mentioned on another occasion that some people say: whatever is God's decree is good, and evil lies in the (divine) destiny (qadar). Thus God decreed that fire has benefit for people, because it is light, and they make it a provision in travels and other things, as God mentioned; and water has the benefit of drinking. But the benefit of fire is only completed by intense heat, and of water by strong flowing; and their being thus necessitates, by God's continuing custom regarding them, that fire burns the garment of the poor and water drowns the sheep of the needy. So the benefit lies in the decree and the harm in the destiny, and this statement has depth. The Sunnah is that we say: "God does what He wills and decides what He desires."

For this reason He said twice, ﴿Indeed, I am a clear warner to you from Him﴾, meaning in the two positions and the two places. We have mentioned many times that the one who negates, when he says there is no Necessary Existent, makes everything contingent, since every existent is contingent; yet God in reality is existent. Thus he has placed Him within the folds of his statement like the contingent things, and so he has associated (partners), making God like other than Him. And the polytheist, when he says that other than Him is a god, it follows from his statement that the god is not a god, according to what we mentioned in the explanation of the argument of mutual prevention (dalalat al-tamana'). Moreover, if there were gods in the heavens and the earth other than God, it would follow the incapacity of each one, so there would be no god in existence at all, and this would negate actual divinity, and so he would be a negator, and the negator is a polytheist, and the polytheist is a negator. Each of the two groups acknowledges that the other is in error, but each, on the other's doctrine, says that his own position is false, and he does not know it. Praise be to God who guided us. His saying, ﴿do not set up﴾, contains a subtle point: it is an indication that the gods are made (majul), not that God is taken. One might say: God is also "taken," by His saying, ﴿so take Him as trustee﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 9]. We answer: the answer to this is evident, and it has already been mentioned in His saying, exalted: ﴿And they took, besides God, gods﴾ [Ya-Sin: 74].

* * *

Then God, exalted, said: ﴿Thus, no messenger came to those before them except that they said, "A sorcerer or a madman."﴾

The exegesis is known from what has preceded, and we have mentioned that it indicates that the mention of narratives is for consolation. However, there is one subtle point here that we will not leave out: this verse is evidence that every messenger was denied, and then questions arise about it.

The first: among the prophets there were some who confirmed the religion of the prophet who came before them, and the people remained upon what they were upon, such as the prophets of the Children of Israel for a period. And how is it, since Adam, when he was sent, was not denied?

The second: what is the wisdom in God's decree that the messengers be denied, when He did not send a messenger with such multiplicity and variety of miracles that his contemporaries would believe him?

The third: His saying, ﴿no ... came ... except that they said﴾, is evidence that all of them said, "a sorcerer." But this is not so, because there was no messenger who did not have a people who believed in him, and they did not say that.

As for the answer to the first: we say that as for the one who confirmed (the previous religion), we do not concede that he is a messenger; rather he is a prophet upon the religion of a messenger, and whoever denies his messenger is necessarily also denying him.

As for the answer to the second: God sends a messenger only when people have need, and that occurs when unbelievers appear in the world, and unbelief does not appear except when ignorance is abundant. Moreover, God, exalted, does not send a messenger when belief in him is necessary, for otherwise belief in him would be the belief of despair and would not be accepted; and the ignorant person, if the one who makes clear to him is not in utmost clarity, does not accept him, and remains in the entanglement of misguidance. So this is a decree that has been necessitated by God's decree upon creation in this manner. We have mentioned on another occasion that some people say: whatever is God's decree is good, and evil lies in the (divine) destiny (qadar). Thus God decreed that fire has benefit for people, because it is light, and they make it a provision in travels and other things, as God mentioned; and water has the benefit of drinking. But the benefit of fire is only completed by intense heat, and of water by strong flowing; and their being thus necessitates, by God's continuing custom regarding them, that fire burns the garment of the poor and water drowns the sheep of the needy. So the benefit lies in the decree and the harm in the destiny, and this statement has depth. The Sunnah is that we say: "God does what He wills and decides what He desires."

As for the answer to the third: that is not general, for He did not say, "except that they all said." Rather He said, ﴿except that they said﴾, and since many of them, indeed most of them, were saying it, God, exalted, said, ﴿except that they said﴾. If it is asked: why did He not mention the believers, as He mentioned the deniers, and say, "except that some of them said, 'You have spoken truly,' and some of them said, 'You have lied'"? We say: because the purpose is consolation, and consolation is by means of denial. So it is as if God, exalted, said: "Do not grieve over the denial of your people, for nations before you denied, and messengers were denied."

Then God Most High said: ﴿Have they enjoined this on one another? Nay, they are a rebellious people﴾, that is, by that saying, which is their saying: ﴿A sorcerer or a madman﴾. Its meaning is wonderment, i.e., how they came to agree upon one saying, as though they had colluded over it. Some of them said to others: "Do not say anything but this." Then he said: that was not from collusion; rather, it was for a unifying cause, namely that they were all made affluent (utrifu), so they became self-sufficient, forgot God, and transgressed, and so they denied His messengers. This is like a king who grants respite to the people of a region and imposes nothing upon them, then after a period sits down and summons them to his gate, and it is difficult for them, because of their building of palaces and gardens and beautifying of their lands with fine features; so that leads them to disobedience and to saying that they will obey another king.

* * *

Then God Most High said: ﴿So turn away from them, for you are not to be blamed﴾. This is another consolation, because the Prophet ﷺ, out of the nobility of his character, would attribute to himself a shortcoming, and would say that their not believing was due to my shortcoming in conveying the message; so he would strive hard in warning and conveying. So God Most High said: you have already brought what is incumbent upon you, and turning away from them does not harm you, and their disbelief is not due to any shortcoming on your part. So do not grieve, for you are not to be blamed for any shortcoming; rather, they are the ones to be blamed for their aversion and obstinacy.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 51, verses 55–56:

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And remind, for indeed the reminder benefits the believers﴾. He means: it is not turning away absolutely; rather, turn away, turn toward, turn aside, and call. So turning away does not harm you when it is from them, and reminding benefits only when it is with the believers. There is another meaning in it, subtler than this: when the guide's guidance is beneficial, his reward is greater. When He said ﴿So turn away﴾, a person who imagined might say: then the Prophet (ﷺ) will have no great reward. So He said: "Yes," because among the believers there is abundance, and when you remind them, their guidance increases. The increase of guidance from his words is like the increase of the people's worship. A large group, each of whom prays one or two rak'ahs, and a small group, each of whom prays a thousand rak'ahs: the worship in quantity is like the worship in the increase of number. So the guide has a reward for the worship of every person who is guided, and the reward of the one who is guided is not diminished. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And indeed for you there is a reward﴾ [al-Qalam: 3], that is: even if you turn away, because of the benefit of the believers, and even in the state of your turning away from the obstinate. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿for indeed the reminder benefits the believers﴾ admits of several aspects:

The first: that it means the strengthening of their certainty, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿that they may increase in faith﴾ [al-Fath: 4], and He said: ﴿As for those who believed, it has increased them in faith﴾ [al-Tawbah: 124], and He said: ﴿And He increased them in guidance and gave them their piety﴾ [Muhammad: 17].

The second: it benefits the believers who come after you. So, when you increase the reminding by repetition, that is transmitted from you by successive narration (tawatur), and whoever comes after you of the believers benefits from it.

The third: that if the reminder brings about the faith of a disbeliever, then it has benefited a believer, because he has become a believer. And if it does not bring about faith, it produces a good deed, and that is added to the good deeds of the believers, so they benefit. This is what has been said regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that is the Garden which you have been given as an inheritance﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 72].

* * *

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me﴾. This verse contains many benefits, and we shall mention them comprehensively. We say: as for its connection to what precedes it, there are several aspects.

The first: when He said ﴿And remind﴾, He meant the utmost extent of reminding, which is that creation is for nothing but worship. So the purpose of bringing man into existence is worship. Remind them of it, and inform them that everything other than it is a waste of time.

The second: we have mentioned repeatedly that the occupation of the prophets is confined to two matters: the worship of Allah and the guidance of creation. When He said ﴿So turn away from them, for you are not to be blamed﴾, He explained that guidance may lapse when there is despair and no one to be guided, but worship is obligatory, and the absolute creation is for it, and the absolute creation is not for guidance. So you are not to be blamed if you perform the worship, which is the foundation, when you abandon guidance after exerting effort in it.

The third: when He explained the state of those before them in denial, He mentioned this verse to clarify the evil of their conduct, in that they abandoned the worship of Allah, although they were created only for worship.

As for the exegesis, there are several issues:

The first issue: the angels are also among the categories of the obligated (mukallafun), and Allah did not mention them, although the greatest benefit in bringing them into existence is worship. This is why He said: ﴿Rather, they are honored servants﴾ [al-Anbiya': 26], and He said, exalted is He: ﴿They do not disdain from His worship﴾ [al-A'raf: 206]. So what is the wisdom in this?

We say: the answer to it has several aspects.

The first: we have mentioned in some of the aspects that the connection of the verse to what precedes it is a demonstration of the ugliness of what the disbelievers do by abandoning that for which they were created, and this is specific to the jinn and mankind, because disbelief is more prevalent among the jinn, and the disbelievers among them are more numerous than the believers, as we have explained, since the aim is to demonstrate their ugliness and the evil of their conduct.

The second: the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent to the jinn as well. So when He said, "And remind them" with what they are reminded of, namely that creation is for worship, He specified his community by the mention, that is, the mention of the jinn and mankind.

The third: the worshippers of idols used to say that Allah, the Great in status, created the angels and made them those brought near, so they worship Allah, and He created them for His worship. As for us, because of the lowness of our rank, we are not fit to worship Allah, so we worship the angels, and they worship Allah. So Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me﴾, and He did not mention the angels because the matter concerning them was agreed upon among the people, so He mentioned what was disputed.

The fourth: it has been said that the word "jinn" encompasses the angels, because the root of "jinn" is concealment (istitar), and they are hidden from creation. On this basis, the mention of the jinn first is because the angels are included among them, and because they are more abundant in worship and more sincere in it.

The fifth: some people have said that whenever Allah mentions creation, it involves measurement in body and time. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days﴾ [al-Furqan: 59], and He said: ﴿He created the earth in two days﴾ [Fussilat: 9], and He said: ﴿I created with My two hands﴾ [Sad: 75], and so on. And what He did not mention with the word of command (amr), He said: ﴿Indeed, His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin: 82], and He said: ﴿Say, "The soul is of the affair of my Lord"﴾ [al-Isra': 85], and He said, exalted is He: ﴿Unquestionably, to Him belong creation and command﴾ [al-A'raf: 54]. The angels, like the spirits, are from the world of command: He brought them into existence without the passage of time. So His saying ﴿And I did not create﴾ is an indication of those who are of the world of creation, and so the angels do not enter into it. This is false, because of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Creator of everything﴾ [al-Ra'd: 16]. So the angel is from the world of creation.

The second issue: why is the jinn placed before mankind? We say there are several aspects.

The first: some of them have passed in the first issue.

The second: worship is either secret or open, and secret worship has a merit over open worship. But the worship of the jinn is secret, and great showing-off (riya') does not enter it, whereas the worship of mankind may be entered by showing-off. A person may worship Allah for the sake of his fellow human beings, or worship Allah in order to obtain information from the jinn, or out of fear of them. This is not so for the jinn.

The third issue: the act of Allah, exalted is He, is not for a purpose, for otherwise He would be perfected by the purpose, whereas He is perfect in Himself. So how can the purpose and the cause be understood in the command of Allah? We say: the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school) held to this and said: the acts of Allah, exalted is He, are for purposes, and they exaggerated in denying those who deny this. We, however, say several things about it.

The first: causation (ta'lil) is verbal and semantic. The verbal is what the observer applies the word to, even if it is not in reality for it. Its example: when a king leaves his land and enters the land of an enemy, and in his heart he intends only to tire his own army, then the intended meaning is that, but in the wording it is not valid. If he were to say, "I did not travel except to seek a reward, or to gain a good deed," it would be said: this is nothing, and it is not valid of him. And if someone in a similar situation said, "He went out to take the enemy's land and to terrify him," he would be believed. So verbal causation is making a benefit that is regarded as the cause of an act in which there is that benefit. It is said: he traded for profit, even if in reality it is not for him. Having understood this, we say: realities are not known to people, and what is understood from the texts are their verbal meanings. But when a thing has a benefit, causation by it is valid verbally, and the dispute in reality concerns the wording.

The second: that is an estimation (taqdir), like the expression of wishing and hoping in the speech of Allah, exalted is He. It is as if He says: worship, in the view of creation, is something which, if it were one of your actions, you would say that it is for it. As we said regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿perhaps he will remember﴾ [Ta-Ha: 44], that is, so that it becomes a reminder in your eyes, hoped for. And His saying: ﴿Perhaps your Lord will destroy your enemy﴾ [al-A'raf: 129], that is, his destruction becomes hoped for in your eyes; you say: it has drawn near.

The third: the lam (particle of purpose) may occur in what is not valid as a purpose, as in time. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun﴾ [al-Isra': 78], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So divorce them for their waiting period﴾ [al-Talaq: 1]. The meaning is concomitance (muqaranah). It is the same in all the instances. In that case its meaning is: I joined creation with worship, that is, with the obligation of worship, that is, I created them and imposed worship upon them.

What indicates the impossibility of true causation is that Allah, exalted is He, is independent of benefits, so His act is not for a benefit returning to Him nor to anyone else, because Allah, exalted is He, is able to convey the benefit to others without the intermediary of an action. So the mediation of that is not for the sake of being a cause. And if it is necessary to say that Allah, exalted is He, performs an act which is for an intermediary, not for a cause, then the question is binding upon them. As for the texts, they are more than can be enumerated, and they are of several kinds. Among them are those which indicate that misguidance is by the act of Allah, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He misguides whom He wills﴾ [Fatir: 8], and similar. Among them are those which indicate that all things are by the creation of Allah, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Creator of everything﴾ [al-Ra'd: 16]. Among them are the explicit ones which indicate the contrary, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾ [al-Anbiya': 23], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah does what He wills﴾, ﴿He decides what He intends﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 1]. Exhaustive treatment is delegated to the theologian-jurist (mutakallim usuli), not to the exegete.

The fourth issue: He, exalted is He, said: ﴿O mankind, indeed We created you from male and female and made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13], and He said: ﴿to worship Me﴾. Is there a contradiction between them? We say: it is not so, for Allah, exalted is He, gave as the cause of making them peoples the knowing of one another, whereas here He gave as the cause of their creation the worship. His saying there: ﴿Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13] is evidence for what He mentioned here and is in agreement with it. For whoever is more righteous is more devoted to worship and more sincere in action, so what is sought from him is more perfect in existence, and so he is more noble and more honored. Like a thing whose benefit is a usefulness, some of whose instances are more beneficial in that usefulness. Its example: water, when it is created for purification and drinking, the purest of it is more useful for that benefit, so it is more excellent than other water. Likewise the servant in whom is found what is sought from him in a more eloquent manner.

The fifth issue: what is the worship for which the jinn and mankind were created? We say: it is the glorification of Allah's command and compassion toward the creatures of Allah. These two kinds have not been absent from any law (shar'). As for the specific acts of worship, the laws differ regarding them in form, manner, quantity and quality, time and place, conditions and pillars. Since the glorification fitting to the Lord of Majesty and Honour cannot be known by reason, it is necessary to follow the laws concerning it and to accept the words of the Messengers, peace be upon them. Allah has bestowed favour upon His servants by sending the Messengers and clarifying the paths in both kinds of worship. It has been said that its meaning is: "that they may know Me." It was narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said, concerning his Lord: "I was a hidden treasure, so I desired to be known."

It is as if He says: worship, in the view of creation, is something which, if it were one of your actions, you would say that it is for it. As we said regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿perhaps he will remember﴾ [Ta-Ha: 44], that is, so that it becomes a reminder in your eyes, hoped for. And His saying: ﴿Perhaps your Lord will destroy your enemy﴾ [al-A'raf: 129], that is, his destruction becomes hoped for in your eyes; you say: it has drawn near.

The third: the lam (particle of purpose) may occur in what is not valid as a purpose, as in time. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun﴾ [al-Isra': 78], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So divorce them for their waiting period﴾ [al-Talaq: 1]. The meaning is concomitance (muqaranah). It is the same in all the instances. In that case its meaning is: I joined creation with worship, that is, with the obligation of worship, that is, I created them and imposed worship upon them.

What indicates the impossibility of true causation is that Allah, exalted is He, is independent of benefits, so His act is not for a benefit returning to Him nor to anyone else, because Allah, exalted is He, is able to convey the benefit to others without the intermediary of an action. So the mediation of that is not for the sake of being a cause. And if it is necessary to say that Allah, exalted is He, performs an act which is for an intermediary, not for a cause, then the question is binding upon them. As for the texts, they are more than can be enumerated, and they are of several kinds. Among them are those which indicate that misguidance is by the act of Allah, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He misguides whom He wills﴾ [Fatir: 8], and similar. Among them are those which indicate that all things are by the creation of Allah, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Creator of everything﴾ [al-Ra'd: 16]. Among them are the explicit ones which indicate the contrary, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾ [al-Anbiya': 23], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah does what He wills﴾, ﴿He decides what He intends﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 1]. Exhaustive treatment is delegated to the theologian-jurist (mutakallim usuli), not to the exegete.

The fourth issue: He, exalted is He, said: ﴿O mankind, indeed We created you from male and female and made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13], and He said: ﴿to worship Me﴾. Is there a contradiction between them? We say: it is not so, for Allah, exalted is He, gave as the cause of making them peoples the knowing of one another, whereas here He gave as the cause of their creation the worship. His saying there: ﴿Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13] is evidence for what He mentioned here and is in agreement with it. For whoever is more righteous is more devoted to worship and more sincere in action, so what is sought from him is more perfect in existence, and so he is more noble and more honored. Like a thing whose benefit is a usefulness, some of whose instances are more beneficial in that usefulness. Its example: water, when it is created for purification and drinking, the purest of it is more useful for that benefit, so it is more excellent than other water. Likewise the servant in whom is found what is sought from him in a more eloquent manner.

The fifth issue: what is the worship for which the jinn and mankind were created? We say: it is the glorification of Allah's command and compassion toward the creatures of Allah. These two kinds have not been absent from any law (shar'). As for the specific acts of worship, the laws differ regarding them in form, manner, quantity and quality, time and place, conditions and pillars. Since the glorification fitting to the Lord of Majesty and Honour cannot be known by reason, it is necessary to follow the laws concerning it and to accept the words of the Messengers, peace be upon them. Allah has bestowed favour upon His servants by sending the Messengers and clarifying the paths in both kinds of worship. It has been said that its meaning is: "that they may know Me." It was narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said, concerning his Lord: "I was a hidden treasure, so I desired to be known."

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿I do not desire any provision from them, nor do I desire that they should feed Me﴾. In this there is an answer to a question, namely that creation for a purpose indicates need. So He said: I did not create them so that they would feed Me, and the benefit in it is for them, not for Me. This is because the benefit of a slave with regard to his master is that he earns for him, either by bringing in wealth for him or by guarding wealth for him. This is because if the slave is for earning, the purpose of acquisition in him is evident; and if he is for work, then were it not for the slave, the master would need to hire someone to perform the work for him, and so he would need to spend wealth, whereas the slave guards his wealth for him and spares him from spending, so this is a type of earning. Therefore He, exalted is He, said: ﴿I do not desire any provision from them, nor do I desire that they should feed Me﴾, meaning: I am not like the masters who seek service from their slaves; rather, they are the ones who profit by their worship. There is another aspect to this, which is to say that this is an affirmation that they were created for worship. This is because an act, by custom, must have some benefit, but slaves are of two kinds.

Page 201

One kind of them is for majesty and beauty, like the mamluks of kings: the king feeds them, gives them drink, grants them the distant lands of the countries, and bestows upon them the new after the old. What is desired from them is honour and standing before him, and placing the right hand upon the left in his presence. Another kind is for benefiting from them in obtaining provisions or in arranging them. So He, exalted is He, said: I created them, so there must be some benefit in them. Let them reflect upon themselves: are they of the kind from whom the obtaining of provision is demanded, and they are not such? So "I do not desire any provision from them." Or are they of those from whom the preparation of food is demanded, like the cook and the table-server who brings food near, and they are not such? So "nor do I desire that they should feed Me." Therefore they are slaves of the first kind, in that they should not abandon honour. In this there are subtle points which we mention in questions:

The first question: What is the benefit in repeating the two desires, and does one who does not desire provision from anyone not desire that he feed him? We say: it is for what we mentioned before, namely that a master may demand from the slave earning for him, which is seeking provision from him, and a master may have abundant wealth so that he needs no earning, but he demands from him the fulfilment of his needs with his own wealth and the bringing of food before him from his own property. So the Master said: I do not desire that, nor this.

The second question: Why did He put the seeking of provision before the seeking of feeding? We say: this is by way of ascent, like the saying of one who says: I do not seek help from you, nor from one who is stronger, and it is not reversed; and one says: so-and-so is honoured by the amirs, rather by the sultans, and it is not reversed. So here He said: I do not seek from you provision, nor what is less than that, which is the placing of food before the master, for that is a matter much sought from servants, even if earning is not sought from them.

The third question: If He had said "I do not desire from them that they provide for Me, and I do not desire from them any food," would this benefit be obtained? We say: according to what has been detailed, no. This is because through earning one seeks wealth, not the act itself. If he is occupied with work but no wealth results for him, he is not like one for whom wealth results; and if he is not occupied, like the earning slave who abandons work for his need and finds a means by which the master is satisfied, when his work is earning. But as for one from whom the act is desired for the act's own sake, like the hungry man who sends his slave to bring food and he busies himself with taking money from a source, perhaps the master will not be pleased with that. The purpose of provision is wealth, so He did not say it with the wording of the act; and the purpose of feeding is the act itself, so it was mentioned with the wording of the act. And He did not say "I do not desire from them any food," despite what the two wordings have of eloquence and grandeur, for the sake of variety.

The fourth question: If the meaning is what you have mentioned, what is the benefit of feeding and singling it out for mention, given that the purpose is the negation of seeking any act from them other than honour? We say: when He generalised in the first demand He sufficed with His saying "from provision," for it conveys generality, and He alluded to honour by mentioning feeding. This is because the lowest degree of acts is that the master seeks help from his slave or his slave-girl in preparing the matter of food; and the negation of the lower entails the negation of the higher by way of priority. So it is as if He, exalted is He, said: "I do not desire from them" any substance or any work.

The fifth question: According to what I have mentioned, the demands are not confined to what He mentioned, for a master may buy a slave neither for seeking work from him, nor for seeking provision, nor for honour, but buys him for trade and profit through him. We say: the generality of His saying "I do not desire from them any provision" encompasses that, for whoever buys a slave to trade with him has sought provision from him.

The sixth question: "Mā urīdu" in Arabic conveys negation in the present, and singling out by mention implies negation of what is other than what is mentioned; but God, exalted is He, does not desire provision from them neither in the present nor in the future. So why did He not say "lā urīdu minhum min rizqin" and "lā urīdu"? We say: the particle "mā" is not for negation in the present, nor for negation in the future. Thus the speaker, when he says "so-and-so does not do this act" while he is in the act, is not truthful; but if he abandons it and is free from his saying, the speaker is truthful. If he says "he does not do it" it would not be truthful in the case we described. Its example: if a person is in prayer and someone says, "he does not pray," look at him; if the observer looks at him while he has cut off his own prayer, it is correct to say "you do not pray"; but if someone says "he does not pray" at that moment, it would not be true. Once you know this, each of the two words for negation has its particular scope, but negation in the present is more fitting, because by "the present" is meant the lower world, and the future relates to the matter of the Hereafter. The world and its affairs are all in the present state. So His saying "mā urīdu" means, in this present state which is the hour of this world; and it is known that after death a servant is not fit to be asked for provision or work. So His saying "mā urīdu" conveys general negation; had He said "lā urīdu" it would not have conveyed that.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 51, verse 58:

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Provider, the Possessor of strength, the Firm.﴾ This is a justification (ta'lil) for the two matters mentioned previously. His saying "He is the Provider" justifies not seeking provision, and His saying "the Possessor of strength" justifies not seeking work. This is because whoever seeks provision is poor and needy, and whoever seeks work from others is incapable and has no strength. So it is as if He is saying: "What I want from them of provision, I am the Provider; and what I want of work, I am strong."

There are several points (mabahith) here.

The first: He said "I do not want" (ma uridu) and did not say "I am the Provider," but spoke in the manner of reporting about an absent party: "Indeed, Allah." What is the wisdom in this? We say: it has been narrated that the Prophet ﷺ recited "Indeed, I am the Provider" (inni ana al-razzaq), as you have mentioned. As for the well-known recitation, there are several aspects (wujuh) to it.

The first: the meaning is "Say, O Muhammad: Indeed, Allah is the Provider."

The second: this is from the device of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), a return from speaking in the first person to speaking in the third person. There is a benefit here: the name Allah indicates that He is the Provider. This is because al-Ilah means "the one worshipped," as we have mentioned many times, and we relied on the saying of the Exalted: ﴿and [to] abandon you and your gods﴾ [al-A'raf: 127], meaning your objects of worship. When Allah is the one worshipped and He provides for the servant, He employs him without earning, since his provision is incumbent upon the master. Here, when He said: ﴿I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me﴾, He made clear that He has chosen them for Himself and for His worship, and their provision is incumbent upon Him. So He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Provider﴾ using the name Allah, which indicates that He is the Provider. Had He said "Indeed, I am the Provider," the correspondence you mentioned would have been achieved, but the benefit we have mentioned would not.

The third: "Say" (qul) may be understood as implied before His saying: ﴿what I want from them﴾, its estimated form being "Say, O Muhammad: What I want from them of provision." This would be similar in meaning to His saying: ﴿Say: I do not ask you any wage for it﴾ [al-Furqan: 57]. In this case, His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Provider﴾ is part of the Prophet's ﷺ speech, and He did not say it (as a separate statement) but said: ﴿the Possessor of strength﴾. This is because the intent is to affirm what preceded, namely not wanting provision and not seeking help from others. However, for not seeking provision, it is not sufficient that the one who is independent of need can provide for someone, since many people provide for their children and others while also seeking provision, and a king provides for his soldiers while also seeking provision. When much provision comes from someone, the seeking from him diminishes, because one who seeks provision from one who provides abundantly is not sought for provision from his provision. Therefore that intended meaning would not be achieved except by emphasizing the description of provision, so He said: ﴿the Provider﴾ (al-Razzaq, with intensive form). As for what suffices for not seeking help from others, it is less than that: when the strong one is at the utmost degree of strength, he helps others; if he is below that, he does not help others nor seek their help; and if he is below that, he seeks help to some extent, and the degrees differ after that. When He said: ﴿and I do not want them to feed Me﴾, the explanation of strength itself sufficed, so He said: ﴿the Possessor of strength﴾, to convey the meaning of strength (quwwa) rather than the plural forces (quwan). This is because dhu is not used for a description that is necessary and evident. Thus one says of a human: dhu mal (possessor of wealth) and mutamawwil (wealthy), dhu jamal (possessor of beauty) and jamil (beautiful), dhu khuluq hasan (possessor of good character) and khaliq (of good disposition), and other such things that do not necessarily and evidently belong to him. One does not say of three "possessor of oddness" (dhat fardiyya), nor of four "possessor of evenness" (dhat zawjiyya). For this reason it does not occur in the real attributes that are not derived from actions, and therefore one does not hear "dhu al-wujud" (possessor of existence), "dhu al-hayah" (possessor of life), nor "dhu al-'ilm" (possessor of knowledge) in reference to God. But one says of a human "dhu 'ilm" (possessor of knowledge) and "dhu hayah" (possessor of life), because these are accidents (a'rad) in him that are accidental, not evident necessities. And in attributes of action, one says "Allah the Exalted is dhu al-fadl (possessor of bounty) abundantly, and dhu al-khalq (possessor of creation) sparingly," because dhu kadha means "its owner and its lord," and companionship (suhba) does not imply necessity, let alone evident necessity. What supports this is that He, the Exalted, said: ﴿and above every possessor of knowledge is one who knows﴾ [Yusuf: 76], so He made others "possessors of knowledge" and described Himself with the active participle "knowing" (alim). Thus there is a difference between "dhu al-'ilm" and "'alim," and likewise between "dhu al-quwwa" and "qawiyy." It is also supported by His saying: ﴿So Allah seized them; indeed, He is Strong, severe in punishment﴾ [Ghafir: 22], and His saying: ﴿Allah is Subtle with His servants; He provides for whom He wills, and He is the Strong, the Mighty﴾ [al-Shura: 19], and His saying: ﴿I and My messengers will surely overcome; indeed, Allah is Strong and Mighty﴾ [al-Mujadila: 21]. This is because in these instances the intent was to explain the performance of great acts, whereas the intent here is the absence of need. One who does not need others is sufficed with some measure of strength, but one who acts independently by himself must have great strength, because the absence of need may come about by abandoning the action and being independent of it. If this inquiry were presented in the context of answering a questioner about the difference between His saying "dhu al-quwwa" here and "qawiyy" in those other places, it would have been better. If it is said: He, the Exalted, has said: ﴿So that Allah may know who supports Him and His messengers unseen; indeed, Allah is Strong and Mighty﴾ [al-Hadid: 25], and in it is what I mentioned of meaning. This is because His saying "Strong" (qawiyy) is to show that He does not need support, and He only wants to know so that He may reward the helper; but the absence of need for support is sufficed by some strength. So why did He not say "Indeed, Allah is dhu al-quwwa"? We say: in it, He, the Exalted, said "who supports Him and His messengers," and its meaning is that He makes His messengers independent of need, and He does not seek their support from His creatures in order to make them incapable, but seeks it for the reward of the helpers, not because those seeking support are in need. Otherwise, Allah the Exalted promised them victory when He said: ﴿And Our word had already preceded for Our servants, the messengers; indeed, they would be the victorious﴾ [al-Saffat: 171]. And when He mentioned the messengers, He said "qawiyy," so that this would be a strengthening of the closeness of His believing messengers, and a consolation for their hearts and the hearts of the believers.

The second point: He said "al-Matin (the Firm)." This is because "dhu al-quwwa," as we have explained, indicates only that He has some strength, so He added to the description by clarifying it with one who has steadfastness that does not waver. Matin is of the same root as the lexical and semantic origin of "matn," since the matn (core/base) of a thing is its foundation upon which its stability rests, and the matn is the back upon which the body's structure rests. Firmness (matana) with strength is like might (izza) with strength, in that Allah the Exalted, in places where He mentions strength, mentions might, and says: ﴿Strong, Mighty﴾ [al-Hadid: 25], and says: ﴿the Strong, the Mighty﴾.

There is a subtle point in this that supports what we have mentioned about qawiyy and dhu al-quwwa. The matin is the steadfast one who does not waver, and the 'aziz is the dominant one. In the matin is that he is not overcome, not subdued, and not defeated; and in the 'aziz is that he overcomes, subdues, and makes feet slip. Might (izza) is more perfect than firmness (matana), just as the strong (qawiyy) is more perfect than the possessor of strength (dhu al-quwwa). So He paired the more perfect with the more perfect and what is below it with what is below it. If you look at it with the proper look and reflect with the proper reflection, you will see in the Book of Allah the Exalted subtleties that alert you to the stubbornness of the deniers and the ugliness of the denial of the obstinate.

Then God Most High said: ﴿Indeed, for those who wronged there is a portion like the portion of their companions, so let them not ask Me to hasten.﴾ ﴿So woe to those who disbelieved, from their day which they are promised.﴾

Page 204

It is connected to what precedes it, because God Most High explained that whoever places himself in a position of worshipping other than God has placed a thing in other than its proper place, and so he is a wrongdoer. Thus He said: when it is established that mankind and jinn were created for worship, then those who wronged by worshipping others will have a ruin like the ruin of those who came before them. This is because a thing which goes out of the benefit that is sought from it is not kept, even if it is in a place where the space is cleared of it. Do you not see that the beast which no longer benefits anyone, through death or sickness, is removed from the stable, and the food which rots is discarded and the vessel is emptied of it? Likewise the disbeliever, when he wrongs and places himself in other than his proper place, goes out of benefit; so it is fitting to clear the place of him and the ruin is rightly brought down upon him. In the exegesis there are issues:

The first issue: concerning what the fa' (فاء, the particle "fa", "then/so") is connected to, and we have already mentioned to you the manner of its connection.

The second issue: What is the relation of the "dhunub" (ذَنُوب, a full bucketful)? We say: the punishment is poured upon them, as if He, Most High, said: We pour upon their heads a bucketful like the bucketful that was poured upon the heads of those (earlier people). Another aspect: the Arabs drew water from the wells in turns, a bucket after a bucket, and that was at the time of their good life. So it is as if God Most High said: ﴿Indeed, for those who wronged﴾ from the world and its good things, ﴿a dhanub﴾ meaning a full portion, and they will have no share of it in the Hereafter, just as was the state of their companions, who drew a bucketful and then left it. On this view, the dhanub is not a punishment or a ruin, but rather the abundance of life, and this is more fitting to the Arabic language. As for His words: ﴿so let them not ask Me to hasten﴾, the provision, as long as it has not been completed, does not allow the term to come.

Then He repeated what was mentioned at the beginning of the surah, saying: ﴿So woe to those who disbelieved, from their day which they are promised.﴾

All praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds, and may God bless our master Muhammad, his family and all his companions.
